articles.title: Progressives fume at Hakeem Jeffries for saying Democrats won't 'get even' with Trump
articles.summary: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said Democrats should focus on lowering costs instead of getting even, but critics say accountability and delivering re...
articles.body:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., drew progressive criticism Wednesday after saying Democrats should focus on lowering costs following their midterm victories instead of getting "even" with the Trump administration.

"The American people don't want us to get even; they want us to get things done on their behalf because life is way too expensive," Jeffries said on MS NOW's "Morning Joe." "We ran on affordability. We won on affordability, and now it's our job to govern on affordability."

Many progressives want Democrats, now that they will have majorities in the House and Senate, to launch investigations into President Donald Trump , his family and government officials.

Princeton historian Kevin Kruse criticized Jeffries, who is poised to become the next speaker of the House, while sharing a separate House Oversight Democrats post warning, "Lawyer up."

"As disheartening as Jeffries' comments were, remember that other House Democrats actually understand the moment and are ready to meet it," Kruse said in a Bluesky post .

University of Michigan education professor Ebony Elizabeth Thomas also rejected Jeffries' framing, describing accountability as a matter of justice.

"I say this with all love, Brother Leader Jeffries: No," Thomas said in a post responding to the clip . "And it's not (just) retribution. It's restorative justice."

The Oversight Committee is expected to be chaired by Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who was featured in the video put out by the committee's Democrats.

Progressive commentator Brian Tyler Cohen said delivering for voters and investigating abuses of power should work together.

"As content creators, we hear from huge, diverse audiences, and they all want the same thing: a government that works for them, lower costs, leaders who listen and accountability when people abuse their power," he said in a statement to Fox News Digital .

"Delivering results and pursuing accountability go hand in hand, provided investigations follow the evidence and serve the public.

"Creators helped people get involved in this election, and we're going to keep those conversations going, helping audiences stay informed and judge whether their elected leaders are delivering."

The discussion followed Democrats' early warnings about using their anticipated investigative powers.

Jeffries also addressed accountability during Wednesday's interview, saying Democrats should pursue facts, apply the law and follow the Constitution while holding wrongdoers responsible.

In an August CNN interview , he identified the Judiciary and Oversight committees as taking the lead on accountability. He declined to rule impeachment in or out.

"As we've done in the past, whenever there have been moments of accountability that we've had to lead on, we are guided by three principles: follow the facts, apply the law and be guided by the United States Constitution," Jeffries said.

The White House said Trump remained willing to work with Democrats while criticizing the prospect of investigations targeting his administration.

"As the president has said, he's willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans. If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital.

A White House official separately warned that the administration retained federal powers as Democrats prepared to pursue investigations and subpoenas.

"If crazed Democrats want to abuse their power and politicize their process of investigations, subpoenas and destroying lives, they should be reminded that we still control the federal government and all of its powers," the official said.

Media Research Center President David Bozell separately criticized Democrats' campaign message and accused news organizations of shielding the party from scrutiny.

"People want to talk about Trump defying norms? I think Democrats just defied a norm: They ran and won on … nothing," Bozell said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"The media aided and abetted. They were relentlessly negative. They refused to cover any good news. They buried every wart within Democrats' ranks. And today they will be right back at it."

Fox News Digital reached out to Jeffries for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

articles.title: Republicans call for Trump to change course after midterm drubbing
articles.summary: By Nandita Bose, Jarrett Renshaw and Bo Erickson WASHINGTON, Nov 4 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump faced pressure from Republicans on Wednesday to change...
articles.body:
Vice President Vance Campaigns In New York And Ohio For Republican Candidates

By Nandita Bose, Jarrett Renshaw and Bo Erickson

WASHINGTON, Nov 4 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump faced pressure from Republicans on Wednesday to change course after a midterm election rout handed Democrats control of Congress and voters rejected his handpicked candidates in key ‌races.

Republican allies and strategists called for Trump to shake up his White House personnel, restore discipline and scrap policies they blamed ‌for the losses, including the Iran war and tariffs, as his presidency enters its final years.

Veteran Republican strategist John Feehery called the results a "huge disaster" for Trump.

"He needs to clean house," ​Feehery said. "Every day from this point forward, he's becoming more and more lame."

But Trump showed little indication that he viewed the election outcome as a reason to change direction.

"I don't view it as a hit on me," he told Fox News late on Tuesday.

Democrats will now have the power to block Trump's legislation, investigate his administration and challenge his nominees. That is expected to push Trump, who has already used executive authority aggressively, toward an even greater reliance ‌on unilateral action.

He will also have to decide whether ⁠to double down on an agenda that some Republicans fear has become a political liability, particularly for potential successors eyeing White House bids in 2028.

Vice President JD Vance, who is viewed as Trump's likely political heir, appeared to put some ⁠distance between himself and the president on Wednesday, blaming the Iran war for the midterm losses. Such breaks could become more common if Republicans conclude Trump's longtime grip on the party's voters is weakening, strategists and party officials said.

WHITE HOUSE BRACES FOR STAFF SHAKE-UP, INVESTIGATIONS

Inside the White House, senior aides were bracing for ​staff departures, ​possible Cabinet changes and Democratic investigations, according to a senior official who spoke ​on condition of anonymity.

"It absolutely sucks to be here right ‌now," the official said. "Morale is as low as it can get."

The official said internal polling had warned six weeks before the election that Republicans were headed for losses in both chambers, but Trump refused to change course on Iran despite warnings about the political consequences.

"Ultimately, he just didn't care," the official said. "He refused to listen to anyone."

Trump acknowledged late on Tuesday that the eight-month-old Iran war had hurt Republican candidates but defended his decision to launch the conflict.

Republican concerns extended beyond the war. In focus groups conducted for competitive Senate races in places like Michigan and Iowa, national Republican ‌political advisers grew increasingly concerned this summer as more Republican and independent voters ​voiced opposition to the president's focus on the White House ballroom and Washington renovations, a Republican ​political adviser said.

"If Trump spends the next two years talking about ​this same shit, we will get shellacked again in the next election," the adviser said.

Yet on Wednesday, Trump gathered ‌reporters for an impromptu visit to the ballroom construction site ​and defended the time he has ​devoted to the project.

The White House also struck a defiant public tone, posting a photograph of Trump on social media with the message: "PSA: TRUMP IS STILL YOUR PRESIDENT."

Trump still holds considerable power. Reuters previously reported that the White House has ​spent months preparing executive actions on immigration, tariffs, ‌housing and federal spending that could allow him to advance parts of his agenda despite Democratic opposition.

But executive authority will not ​be able to shield the administration from congressional probes.

"Nobody wants to deal with the investigations," the official said.

(Reporting by Nandita Bose, ​Jarrett Renshaw and Bo Erickson; Editing by Colleen Jenkins and Nia Williams)

articles.title: Lula reúne ministros e economistas após BC manter taxa de juros | G1
articles.standfirst: Além de Dario Durigan, vão participar da reunião Geraldo Alckmin, os ex-ministros Fernando Haddad e Guido Mantega e os economistas Luciano Coutinho e Laura Carvalho.
articles.summary: Lula reúne economistas e o ministro Dario Durigan para discutir ajuste fiscal e metas econômicas após o Banco Central interromper o ciclo de queda dos juros.
articles.body:
O presidente Lula convocou o ministro da Fazenda, Dario Durigan, ex-ministros e economistas do PT para discutir nesta quinta-feira (5) medidas para a economia depois de o Banco Central interromper o ciclo de corte de juros nesta quarta (4) . A reunião começou por volta de 12h no Palácio da Alvorada.

Conforme o blog apurou, Durigan faria uma fala inicial, com uma visão geral do estado da economia neste momento e das medidas que sua equipe está analisando para garantir o cumprimento das metas fiscais e a manutenção dos programas sociais.

Foram convidados para a reunião, além de Dario Durigan, o vice-presidente Geraldo Alckmin , os ministros Bruno Moretti (Planejamento), Miriam Belchior (Casa Civil) e Esther Dweck (Gestão), os ex-ministros Fernando Haddad , Aloizio Mercadante e Guido Mantega , além dos economistas Luciano Coutinho, Eduardo Moreira e Laura Carvalho.

Em sua fala, Durigan iria apresentar as medidas em estudo que devem prever aumento de contingenciamento de gastos e travas no aumento de gastos obrigatórios, como saúde e educação, mas sem redução de verbas.

Segundo interlocutores de Durigan, o objetivo é fazer um ajuste fiscal consistente e gradual, para garantir uma redução da taxa de juros e a manutenção no longo prazo de todas as políticas sociais do governo Lula.

Em entrevista a jornalistas, ele evitou, entretanto, criticar a decisão do Copom que interrompeu o ciclo de corte da Selic ao manter a taxa estável em 13,75% ao ano.

"Eu não vou fazer esse tipo de comentário valorativo, mas, mais uma vez, a taxa de juros no Brasil é muito alta, o esforço que nós temos que fazer no governo Lula 4 é dar as condições corretas, estruturais, os corretos estímulos para que a gente diminua a taxa de juros", disse o ministro.

A reunião com Lula acontece num momento em que petistas criticam o Banco Central pelos juros altos e pedem mudanças na política monetária.

Além disso, rejeitam um ajuste fiscal forte. Enquanto isso, o mercado está na espera do anúncio de medidas de contenção de despesas pelo governo.

Segundo um banqueiro, o mercado não quer um "tesouraço", como prometeu Flávio Bolsonaro, mas um plano crível e consistente de redução do crescimento das despesas para garantir estabilidade na economia .

Caso contrário, diz o banqueiro, o país vai conviver com crescimento baixo, falta de recursos para programas e pressões inflacionárias .

articles.title: Maioridade penal: crimes hediondos são minoria entre adolescentes | G1
articles.standfirst: Dados do Sinase mostram que roubo e tráfico concentram 57% dos registros de 2025. O alcance da mudança na lei depende de qual proposta prevalecer no Congresso: uma inclui o tráfico de drogas, a outra não.
articles.summary: Levantamento do Sinase mostra que roubo e tráfico somam 57% das infrações, gerando impasse sobre o alcance da redução da maioridade penal na PEC da Segurança Pública.
articles.body:
Os crimes mais citados no debate sobre a redução da maioridade penal são minoria entre os atos atribuídos a adolescentes no sistema socioeducativo. Em 2025, homicídio, estupro, latrocínio, feminicídio e tortura, crimes considerados hediondos por lei, somaram 14,5% dos 13.367 atos infracionais registrados entre jovens em restrição ou privação de liberdade no Brasil , segundo o levantamento anual do Sistema Nacional de Atendimento Socioeducativo (Sinase).

Roubo (29,1%) e tráfico de drogas (27,9%), juntos, responderam por 57%.

A diferença importa porque o Congresso discute justamente se a redução deve valer só para crimes hediondos , ou seja, que a legislação brasileira considera de gravidade extrema (leia mais abaixo) . Os dois atos infracionais mais frequentes ficam numa zona cinzenta: roubo só é hediondo em algumas circunstâncias; o tráfico é equiparado a hediondo pela Constituição, mas não aparece na lei que lista esses crimes.

Por isso, o alcance da mudança depende da redação do texto. Se valer só para os crimes listados na Lei 8.072/1990, os atos que se enquadram (estupro, latrocínio e sua tentativa, e feminicídio) representam 4,9% do total. Se incluir os equiparados, só o tráfico acrescenta quase 28%.

O tema voltou ao centro do debate no Senado. Ao aprovar a PEC da Segurança Pública na terça-feira (3), os senadores decidiram separar do texto a questão da maioridade penal. O tema vem sendo tratado em duas emendas, que apresentam caminhos distintos para o assunto:

PEC 19/2026: É a emenda da oposição, que tem como primeiro signatário o senador Rogério Marinho (PL-RN). Propõe reduzir a maioridade para 16 anos em todos os crimes. Ela também prevê 14 anos para crimes hediondos, tortura, tráfico de drogas, terrorismo, organização criminosa, associação criminosa e outros definidos em lei.

PEC 19/2026, do senador Rogério Marinho — Foto: Reprodução/Senado Federal

PEC 20/2026: Emenda do senador Camilo Santana (PT-CE), reduz a maioridade para 16 anos apenas nos crimes “formalmente” hediondos.

PEC 20/2026, do senador Camilo Santana — Foto: Reprodução/Senado Federal

O líder do MDB no Senado, Eduardo Braga (AM), apresentou um pedido para acelerar a votação das PECs que reduzem a maioridade penal. Alcolumbre, porém, indicou que pretende respeitar a tramitação já iniciada pela Câmara dos Deputados.

Na Câmara, o tema é discutido em uma PEC própria, analisada por uma comissão especial. A expectativa é que o colegiado vote o parecer do deputado Mendonça Filho (PL-PE) entre o fim de novembro e o início de dezembro.

A palavra "formalmente" muda o alcance da proposta. A Lei 8.072/1990 lista os crimes hediondos. Já a Constituição, no artigo 5º, equipara a eles o tráfico de drogas, a tortura e o terrorismo, que recebem o mesmo tratamento sem estar naquela lista.

Segundo o advogado Felippe Angeli, coordenador de advocacy do JUSTA e integrante da Comissão de Segurança Pública da OAB-SP, o termo “formalmente” na emenda de Camilo Santana (PT) restringe a mudança aos crimes da Lei 8.072. Na prática, isso deixaria de fora os equiparados, entre eles o tráfico.

O tráfico de drogas responde por quase 28% dos atos registrados pelo Sinase . Pela emenda da oposição, ele passaria a ser julgado como um "crime de adulto" a partir dos 14 anos.

“Quando você fala de tráfico de drogas, você está falando basicamente de um terço de todos os atos infracionais que estão acontecendo hoje”, afirma Angeli.

Atos infracionais de adolescentes — Foto: Arte/g1

O advogado Felippe Angeli aponta um risco adicional: a distinção entre usuário e traficante de drogas. “Historicamente, a gente vê uma má caracterização tanto da polícia quanto da Justiça criminal em situações relacionadas seja ao consumo, seja ao tráfico de drogas”, diz. Segundo ele, há um viés racial e social nessa classificação: um adolescente flagrado com droga em um bairro nobre tende a ser tratado de forma diferente de outro, na mesma situação, na periferia.

O roubo, ato mais frequente, também ficaria em grande parte fora da emenda de Camilo Santana, porque o roubo simples não é hediondo (veja abaixo quando ele é).

Durante a campanha eleitoral, o presidente Lula, que foi reeleito, declarou pela primeira vez ser favorável à redução da idade penal para 16 anos em crimes hediondos.

“Crime hediondo exige punição. E eu, como cidadão, sou favorável à redução da maioridade penal para 16 anos em casos de crimes hediondos. Segurança pública é coisa séria e precisa ser tratada com responsabilidade, sem distorcer o debate”, escreveu Lula no X.

Para Angeli, a mudança de posição do PT e a emenda de Camilo Santana funcionaram como uma “redução de danos” diante da proposta da oposição, em uma eleição muito disputada e com um tema que tem apoio popular nas pesquisas.

Para Rafael Alcadipani, professor da Fundação Getulio Vargas e especialista em segurança pública, não há evidências de que a maioridade penal vá reduzir a criminalidade, "mesmo porque a quantidade de crimes que são praticados por jovens e que são crimes hediondos é muito pequena".

No entanto, Alcadipani ressalta que uma questão fundamental na discussão é a sensação de justiça e evitar a impunidade.

Angeli avalia que a mudança não terá impacto positivo na segurança pública. Para ele, o efeito pode ser o oposto: o recrutamento de jovens cada vez mais novos pelas facções criminosas.

O professor lembra que o adolescente que comete ato infracional já é responsabilizado. “A internação não é nenhum passeio. É privação da liberdade, é responsabilização”, diz. Segundo ele, o ECA pode ser revisado em lei ordinária para ampliar a resposta a casos excepcionais de crimes graves, sem mexer na Constituição.

“A criança e o adolescente, na imensa maioria dos casos, é vítima, não é agressor”, afirma.

Adolescentes em medidas socioeducativas em meio fechado — Foto: Lara Bernardino - Arte/g1

Hoje, adolescentes que cometem atos infracionais cumprem medidas socioeducativas — e não penas do sistema prisional comum. Essas medidas incluem:

Internação: Privação de liberdade como medida principal

Internação provisória: Custódia temporária antes da sentença

Semiliberdade: Regime parcial com saídas externas

Internação-sanção: Punição por descumprimento de medida

Angeli afirma que pesquisas de opinião registram apoio à redução da maioridade penal e pondera que o grau de conhecimento sobre a proposta também pode influenciar a percepção dos entrevistados, especialmente quando são apresentados detalhes sobre seu funcionamento e alcance.

Na avaliação do advogado, o medo provocado pela crise na segurança pública favorece a simplificação de debates complexos, mesmo quando as mudanças propostas podem produzir efeitos contrários aos pretendidos. Ele afirma ainda que o tema pode ser explorado por lideranças e atores políticos em busca de ganhos eleitorais ou de posicionamento político.

"Muitas vezes, lideranças e atores políticos acabam usando isso em benefício eleitoral ou para obter algum tipo de benefício ou posicionamento político. Acho que é um pouco o que está acontecendo agora", conclui.

São os crimes que a legislação brasileira considera de gravidade extrema e trata com mais rigor. A Constituição prevê a categoria no artigo 5º, inciso XLIII, e a Lei 8.072/1990 define quais são. A lista inclui, entre outros, homicídio qualificado, latrocínio, estupro, feminicídio e extorsão mediante sequestro. Tráfico de drogas, tortura e terrorismo não estão na lista, mas são equiparados pela Constituição.

Quem é condenado por esses crimes não tem direito a fiança, anistia, graça ou indulto. Também precisa cumprir uma parte maior da pena antes de progredir de regime: no mínimo 40% para réus primários e 16% nos crimes comuns sem violência, segundo a Lei de Execução Penal.

Roubo: é hediondo desde o Pacote Anticrime (2019) apenas quando há arma de fogo, restrição da liberdade da vítima ou lesão grave.

Homicídio: só entra na lista quando é qualificado.

Porte de arma: é hediondo apenas quando a arma é de uso proibido.

Tráfico privilegiado: aplicado a réus primários sem ligação com organizações criminosas, não é tratado como hediondo, segundo a Lei de Execução Penal e o Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF).

Hoje, essa classificação não se aplica a adolescentes. Eles respondem pelo Estatuto da Criança e do Adolescente (ECA) e cumprem medidas socioeducativas.

articles.title: TSE permite manter mandato de mulher eleita em chapa com fraude à cota de gênero  | G1
articles.standfirst: Ministros alteraram entendimento da própria corte e destacaram que casos serão analisados individualmente. Única mulher da Corte, ministra Estela Aranha votou contra.
articles.summary: Ministros alteraram entendimento da própria corte e destacaram que casos serão analisados individualmente. Única mulher da Corte, ministra Estela Aranha votou contra.
articles.body:
O Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) decidiu nesta quinta-feira (3) alterar o entendimento da própria Corte sobre as consequências da fraude à cota de gênero nas eleições.

Ficou definido que mulheres eleitas que não tenham envolvimento direto com a fraude podem manter seus mandatos.

Há dez anos, o TSE vem adotando o entendimento de que a fraude derruba toda a chapa e anula todos os votos, com a rejeição do Demonstrativo de Regularidade de Atos Partidários (Drap) da legenda.

🔎 O Drap é o documento que reúne as informações sobre a regularidade da chapa apresentada pelo partido ou federação para disputar a eleição.

A Lei das Eleições estabelece que os partidos precisam garantir pelo menos 30% de candidaturas de cada gênero na composição das listas ( leia mais abaixo ).

O TSE utiliza como critérios para considerar uma candidatura feminina fictícia, por exemplo:

ausência de movimentação de recursos de campanha;

prestação de contas zerada ou ausência de prestação de contas;

falta de participação em atos de campanha, inclusive nas redes sociais; e

demonstração de desinteresse da candidata pela disputa eleitoral.

Com o novo entendimento, chapas que registrarem fraude à cota de gênero nas eleições proporcionais terão os votos das candidaturas fictícias convertidos em votos de legenda, ou seja, computados para o partido. Isso vale para candidaturas a deputado federal, deputado estadual e vereador.

No julgamento, os ministros destacaram que os casos continuarão a ser analisados individualmente e não haverá validação automática dos votos. Inicialmente, esse precedente será aplicado aos casos das eleições de 2022 que ainda estão pendentes de julgamento.

Sessão plenária do TSE - 15/10/2026 — Foto: Antonio Augusto/TSE

Os ministros analisaram um recurso contra a decisão do Tribunal Regional Eleitoral do Amapá (TRE-AP) que rejeitou ações por abuso de poder e suposta fraude à cota de gênero em candidaturas femininas do Podemos para o cargo de deputado estadual no Amapá nas eleições de 2022.

O partido registrou 25 candidaturas, sendo oito de mulheres. Dessas, três foram consideradas fictícias.

O caso começou a ser analisado em junho, teve dois pedidos de vista e foi retomado na sessão desta quinta (5) com o voto da ministra Estela Aranha, única mulher da Corte.

A ministra foi o único voto contrário à alteração do entendimento do TSE. Segundo Estela Aranha, não há uma solução fácil para o caso, mas permitir a validação dos votos em uma chapa na qual a fraude à cota foi reconhecida pode criar instabilidade sistêmica e transformar o Judiciário em "engenheiro de resultado", escolhendo qual candidato está apto ou não a exercer o mandato.

Estela Aranha afirmou ser preocupante punir mulheres que nada têm a ver com as fraudes, mas ponderou que, na prática, a manutenção dos mandatos premiaria quem fraudou as cotas e comprometeria a integridade eleitoral.

"Fechar os olhos para fraude comprovada quando se tem caso de benefício e preservar mandatos por mecanismo de fraudes significa premiar quem burlou a lei. Não se protege participação das mulheres para encobrir candidaturas fictícias. Se esse mecanismo for validado, estará expulsando mulheres de candidaturas reais. A lógica desse raciocínio é devastadora, passa-se a mensagem que vale a pena fraudar", disse.

Relator do caso, o ministro André Mendonça rebateu a colega e disse que é mínima a possibilidade de o novo entendimento retirar espaço de mulheres com candidaturas reais.

Para o ministro, a decisão trata justamente da exigência prevista em lei de garantir ações afirmativas para as mulheres e preservar mandatos obtidos por candidatas que não participaram da fraude.

"Quando se está diante de mulher eleita, sem ter participação alguma na fraude, ela é vítima da fraude, e como consequência punida uma segunda vez. Venceram o obstáculo das fraudes, são eleitas, e agora são vítimas da anulação dos próprios votos obtidos legitimamente", disse o ministro.

Mendonça fez ajustes no voto para incluir sugestões dos colegas. O voto do relator prevaleceu e foi seguido por outros cinco ministros.

O presidente do TSE, Kassio Nunes Marques, que também acompanhou o relator, ressalvou que, em seu entendimento, a mudança deveria ficar restrita às eleições de 2022.

“Daqui a dois anos teremos eleições municipais e podemos estar criando uma evasão para que os diretórios partidários não se animem a realizar uma distribuição equânime de recursos, principalmente em relação às cotas, todas elas e, no caso a cota de candidatas mulheres, e concentrem o esforço em uma só candidata, sabendo que a jurisprudência desta corte poderá se mantida, ser benevolente”, afirmou o ministro.

Nunes Marques ressaltou que as candidaturas das eleições de 2024 deverão ser avaliadas caso a caso nos processos que chegarem à Corte a partir do primeiro semestre de 2027.

“Então o meu voto é, evoluindo nessa jurisprudência, acompanhando o eminente relator para manter a candidatura feminina, porém, limitada à eleição de 2022, com a possibilidade de avançar ainda para as eleições de 24. Teremos ainda esse momento de analisarmos também como ocorreu e em qual medida essas fraudes voltaram a ocorrer nas eleições de 2024”.

articles.title: Selic: PT e ala na equipe de Lula atacam BC após Copom manter juros | G1
articles.summary: A manutenção da taxa Selic em 13,75% motivou ataques do PT ao Banco Central, enquanto o governo Lula busca equilibrar o ajuste fiscal com promessas sociais de campanha.
articles.body:
O PT e parte da equipe do presidente Lula estão atacando o Banco Central, dizendo que o Copom se rendeu ao mercado e parou de cortar a taxa Selic, que ficou em 13,75% ao ano.

Entre petistas e uma ala do governo, há quem defenda, inclusive, que o presidente Lula indique a partir de agora diretores mais alinhados com uma visão de redução dos juros .

Do seu lado, o Copom justifica a interrupção do ciclo de corte de juros pelo cenário de incertezas na área fiscal e pressões sobre a inflação no curto prazo.

O mercado, majoritariamente, já vinha prevendo que o BC iria manter a taxa Selic em 13,75% diante de uma inflação em alta e riscos de as contas públicas seguirem no vermelho.

Até agora, só há promessas de que Lula terá responsabilidade fiscal em seu quarto mandato, mas pouco se sabe sobre o que a equipe econômica irá propor para garantir o cumprimento das metas fiscais, que, no próximo ano, prevê um superávit primário de 0,5% do PIB .

Lula fará um pronunciamento, no próximo domingo, prometendo responsabilidade fiscal, mas também garantindo que não haverá cortes em programas sociais e suas promessas de campanha serão cumpridas. Nas palavras de assessores, não haverá "estelionato eleitoral" no Lula 4.

🔎Estelionato eleitoral é uma expressão usada para definir casos em que um candidato, após eleito, adota medidas contrárias ao que prometeu durante a campanha. Apesar do nome, não é um crime previsto na legislação brasileira.

O vice-líder do governo na Câmara dos Deputados , Lindbergh Farias, disse que o BC sucumbiu às pressões do mercado. Segundo ele, se o Flávio Bolsonaro vencesse, o mercado previa queda dos juros. Se fosse Lula, como foi, a queda dos juros seria interrompida. O que foi formalizado ontem pelo Copom.

O PT chegou a defender, nos últimos dias, uma proposta do economista André Lara Resende, um dos pais do plano real, que previa uma queda da taxa Selic num prazo de doze meses para 7,5% ao ano .

Depois, seria criado um teto para a taxa de juros e para a meta fiscal. A ideia foi criticada por economistas, sob o argumento de que esse plano nunca foi testado em nenhum país e representaria um risco para o país.

O ministro da Fazenda, Dario Durigan, está fechando com sua equipe medidas para garantir o cumprimento do centro da meta fiscal a partir do próximo ano, quando está previsto um superávit primário de 0,5% do Produto Interno Bruto (PIB).

Segundo eles, as propostas devem ser levadas a Lula depois do seu retorno à Turquia, onde participará da reunião da COP 30. Ele viaja no próximo dia 9 de novembro e retorna no dia 12 de novembro.

Em relação às indicações para diretoria do BC, duas vagas estão abertas, de Política Econômica e Organização do Sistema Financeiro.

Em fevereiro, serão abertas mais duas, de Política Monetária e Fiscalização. Dentro do PT, a defesa é que Lula aproveite para indicar diretores do Banco Central mais alinhados a uma política de redução da taxa de juros.

Interlocutores do presidente ouvidos pelo blog dizem, porém, que ele não fará isso .

Seria o mesmo que comprar uma crise com os investidores e sinalizar que o presidente pretende comandar o Banco Central, que tem autonomia para operar sua política monetária.

articles.title: What Trump’s midterms setback could mean for Iran, Israel and Ukraine
articles.summary: The US midterm elections could have consequences far beyond the country’s borders. President Donald Trump has spent nearly two years overturning decades of A...
articles.body:
The US midterm elections could have consequences far beyond the country's borders. President Donald Trump has spent nearly two years overturning decades of American foreign policy, unsettling allies and adversaries alike. Now, both are watching to see how an electoral setback at home will shape his actions abroad.

For Iran, Israel and Ukraine, the stakes go well beyond who controls Congress. The result could influence whether Trump pursues a deal with Tehran or more war, how much Washington's longstanding support for Israel erodes, and how hard he pushes Kyiv to accept terms to end Russia's war.

Democrats will have new tools to challenge Trump. But he still has considerable freedom to act abroad, leaving world leaders with a question: Will defeat make him more willing to compromise, or more determined to get his way?

Here's how the vote could impact Washington's most pressing foreign policy concerns:

Iran gloats, but gets no guarantee of peace

Iran is celebrating Trump's midterm setback, but it is bracing for what comes next: a possible new US strike or a fresh push for a deal.

Trump admitted in a call with Fox News that the war in Iran was partly to blame for the Republicans' losses but Vice President JD Vance was more explicit, saying in a lengthy X post Wednesday that "the reason we lost is the war."

After eight months of striking the region's economic lifelines to turn American voters against the war, Tehran has hailed the Republican loss as a public verdict on it. Trump acknowledged that war-driven price hikes played a role.

"If the US government betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare," parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who has led negotiations with the US, wrote on X.

Tehran is not betting on a change of course in Washington. Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said anyone who believes the results will shift US policy is "deeply mistaken," and officials say Iran's strategy doesn't hinge on American elections as they prepare for more war while intensifying diplomacy.

The risk of escalation is real. Reports that Trump might order new, more intense strikes are fueling anxiety across the region, and Tehran has warned that its retaliation would be much wider in scope than in earlier rounds. This week, Trump told some journalists he is considering striking Iran hard, and others that he has no immediate plans to escalate.

"The Iran war has become a political albatross around his neck, leaving (Trump) with a stark choice: cut a face-saving deal and declare victory, or double down militarily to reclaim the initiative," Ali Vaez of International Crisis Group told CNN. "The danger is that a president weakened at the ballot box may seek redemption on the battlefield."

Diplomacy offers another path. Talks that stagnated over the summer have picked up in the past week, with Tehran sending officials to Qatari mediators who are circulating proposals with Washington. Before the vote, Iran offered to open the Strait of Hormuz within two days if Trump agreed to its seven conditions.

Sanam Vakil of Chatham House said Iran's leadership "might feel vindicated," but that "does not necessarily solve their problems." Trump needs a diplomatic victory yet may be reluctant to appear weak, she said, while Tehran could read his setback as a chance to demand greater concessions. She expects intensified diplomacy alongside military threats, with an interim Strait of Hormuz deal "more realistic" than a comprehensive one.

In Israel, the election day announcement that Trump would abruptly cut off US military aid to the country was the first surprise. The results, with Democrats sweeping both chambers of Congress in what has been called a "blue tsunami," are a five-alarm fire in Israel.

Bipartisan support for Israel in the US had already been eroding, with Democrats outraged at Israel over the death toll in the Gaza war and a growing number of Republicans believing the US has given it too much support.

"The only bipartisan issue right now is criticism of Israel," said Michael Oren, a former Israeli ambassador to the US. "It's an organizing principle for the Democratic Party," he told CNN. "And it's becoming an organizing principle for much of the Republican Party."

Oren said the end of US aid is just the beginning of a process that has only started to play out. He said it's conceivable that the US could end intelligence sharing with Israel and the joint development of critical military systems, such as the vaunted Iron Dome aerial defense system. He also pointed to the United Nations Security Council, where Republican and Democratic presidents have protected Israel with the US veto.

Yaakov Katz, a former editor-in-chief of the Jerusalem Post, warned there is more to come. "What Trump announced about the military aid yesterday is just the tip of the iceberg of what can change – arms sales could be blocked, sanctions will be proposed and joint economic programs defunded," he said on X.

The anti-Israel sentiment only hardened during the Iran war, with segments of the US electorate viewing the joint US-Israel strikes as a war that Netanyahu sold to Trump. Even now, Netanyahu has been pushing to resume strikes on Iran, which would reignite a war that drove gas prices and the cost of living higher and contributed to Republicans' devastating midterm performance.

Netanyahu also faces turmoil at home. In elections a week before the midterms, he lost his majority in parliament, but his main rival, former military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, does not have an outright majority and would likely need to cooperate with Arab parties, who saw record turnout.

Yair Golan, leader of the left-wing Democrats party, warned that Israel "does not have time to waste" in replacing Netanyahu and leading the country away from sanctions and isolation.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky is hoping the the "blue wave" will bolster American support for its defense against Russia's war.

"I am also grateful to the Republicans, but the Democrats speak very clearly about supporting Ukraine and providing assistance to Ukraine," Zelensky said in comments provided in German by broadcaster ZDF, ahead of the telecast of the interview, according to Reuters.

"They speak about renewing the connection between the United States and Europe… Therefore, there is hope that a balance of power will emerge and that we will receive more support."

He added: "If Congress now speaks of strong financial support or military assistance, as Europe is doing and demonstrating today, then that will be something positive that will have an impact on Putin."

For weeks, President Volodymyr Zelensky's relationship with Trump has been in freefall. Trump has demanded Zelensky be replaced; courted energy deals to benefit Russia; and watched as Ukraine's tech and intel dependencies on the US were inexplicably thwarted. And so Kyiv was forced to take a position early: wait, with urgency, for a post-Trump world.

And when it began to dawn on Wednesday, there was little official comment from Kyiv at first, Zelensky perhaps happy for the memes of him, sat with a beer and popcorn in front of the mid-term TV coverage, to do the job for him.

A deputy in his office, Sergiy Kyslytsia, pledged on Ukrainian TV that the country would continue to "develop genuine, normal and stable relations" with whoever is in office, seek Patriot interceptors, and navigate both a new Congress and the likely flurry of executive orders that may try to obviate it.

But there can be no disguising that a crestfallen Trump, and the slow clock now loudly ticking on his worldview and presidency, is in Kyiv's favour. He had claimed a peace was easy to fashion, yet proceeded to punish Ukraine for not agreeing to the demands of its invader. He humiliated, scolded, and then occasionally made up with, Zelensky, while massaged by European allies, aghast at the breakdown in decades of security alliances.

There is still a lot that Ukraine needs Trump and the United States to do. Provide arms, money, and a wider assurance it is on their side. But Kyiv has calculated it cannot depend on Washington, after months of hostility.

There is one downside of the ticking clock however: that Russian President Vladimir Putin determines he has likely a year to pursue, at any cost, the best outcome possible in his war of choice, before the 2028 fight drags Republican policy back to the pro-Ukrainian mainstream. Putin has so far failed to use his apparent great ally, Trump, to secure a battlefield win of note. He may seek to change that while the embers of Trump's authority burn.

articles.title: After midterms, Europe looks beyond Trump
articles.summary: “Everybody is now obliged to look toward the post-Trump era,” a European diplomat told Semafor.
articles.body:
Democrats' sweeping midterm victory could give European allies fresh confidence to push back against President Donald Trump, weakening his leverage over countries that have previously accommodated his demands.

After the midterms, "everybody is now obliged to look toward the post-Trump era," a European diplomat told Semafor.

"In the first two years [of Trump's presidency], we saw a lot of bending the knee by Europeans," said Max Bergmann of the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

But Bergmann predicted that deference could fade: "We're going to see less of that going forward, because there's a sense that they don't need to take it."

Richard Fontaine, CEO of the Center for a New American Security, said allies like the United Kingdom and South Korea may also be less inclined to honor billion-dollar trade agreements negotiated under pressure; instead, they'll have an "incentive" to "play out the clock."

"President Trump has effectively restored American strength on the global stage and strengthened relationships with world leaders," White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly told Semafor.

"The results speak for themselves: fair trade is restored, investments are pouring in, narcoterrorists are eliminated, detained Americans are home, and our homeland is safer. The President will continue to work with anyone to put America first and improve the livelihoods of families across the country," she said.

articles.body:
Seismic political change is coming to Washington, D.C., and as Republicans sift through the wreckage that was Election Night, fingers are pointing in several directions over who's to blame.

The blue tsunami Tuesday tore the GOP's coalition asunder, flipping the balance of power in both chambers heading into the final two years of the Trump administration. And as Republicans search for where things went awry, GOP operatives and insiders told Fox News Digital that it starts at the top with President Donald Trump.

"Look, first and foremost, this is a Trump loss," Dan Eberhart, an oil drilling chief executive officer and prominent Republican donor, told Fox News Digital. "He wanted to be — he wanted people to consider him on the ballot. And unfortunately, as a Republican, that's what we got."

In the Senate, Democrats scored seven pickups on Election Night, with outstanding races in Alaska and Mississippi still waiting to be called. And in the House, Democrats roared back into power with 27 pickups and with several races still outstanding.

The Iran war, ignoring the economic hurt squeezing voters, attacking sitting Republicans and more are on the list of grievances from Republicans reeling in the days after.

The Senate map, in particular, was at one point favorable for Republicans and viewed as an uphill battle for Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and Democrats to put a dent in the GOP's thin, 53-seat majority.

But Trump's decision to go on a "primary revenge tour and antagonizing senators," a GOP aide told Fox News Digital, among several other issues, opened up the field for Democrats to pounce.

Indeed, Trump's handpicked candidates were pummeled in races that were once safe bets for Republicans.

His backing of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., and fight with Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., last year that ultimately led to his retirement and created an opening for Democrats in the Tar Heel State, proved fatal for the GOP, coupled with stunning losses in Maine, Kansas, Ohio and Iowa, kneecapped any chances Republicans had of keeping power in the upper chamber.

"Trump ignored affordability completely," another Republican aide told Fox News Digital. "Ousted good members a la Cornyn, Tillis who knew how to win tough races, and poisoned the base's opinion of our majority with his SAVE Act/filibuster bulls---."

"We had a great map, and he hijacked [it]," they continued.

In the House, where Democrats are on pace to potentially win upward of 250 seats, Fox News Power Rankings projected that Trump's tariffs and the war in Iran were significant drivers for voting blocs leaving the GOP.

One House Republican complained that GOP leaders were too focused on "bluster" rather than "doing the job," though they did not mention Trump by name.

"All the name changes were so unnecessary — Gulf of America, Lake of America, Department of War," the GOP lawmaker said.

A second House Republican rattled off a lengthy list of shortcomings, including the quality and character of "certain candidates," Trump's immigration enforcement, tariffs, general affordability issues, historic midterm headwinds, and "departure from traditional conservatism in favor of populism."

Meanwhile, people in Trump's orbit blamed the candidates themselves.

Trump outside advisor Alex Bruesewitz posted on X that "most Republican candidates this cycle were uninspiring, lazy, and thoroughly ineffective communicators."

"I'm not all that surprised by some of these outcomes," he said.

Meanwhile, some are expecting a massive shift in Trump's base of support in Congress as he heads toward a lame duck likely punctuated by investigations and stalled agendas.

"I think Trump being a lame duck starts today," Eberhart said. "You know, if I'm up in the [2028] cycle, I'm waking up today, I'm against the arch. I'm against the ballroom. I want space from Trump."

articles.title: Vance, DeSantis make quick moves after disastrous GOP midterms jumpstart 2028 race
articles.summary: The vice president’s seemingly straightforward path to succeeding President Donald Trump suddenly looks much murkier.
articles.body:
Vice President JD Vance's seemingly straightforward path to succeeding President Donald Trump suddenly looks much murkier.

The Republican shellacking in Tuesday's midterm elections has quickly triggered a public reckoning within the GOP over Trump's place in the future of the party — one that threatens to complicate Vance's efforts to consolidate party support behind a widely anticipated White House bid.

Vance appeared to recognize the danger Wednesday morning, blaming the party's sweeping losses on the war with Iran and distancing himself from Trump's unpopular foreign policy decisions. In a lengthy post on X , Vance appeared to sketch out what the foundations for his own 2028 platform, centered on ending the war, tackling affordability, refocusing on domestic challenges and reconsidering America's relationship with Israel.

"To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be," he wrote. "Let's take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country."

But there are already signs that there may be a widening lane for someone outside the administration to seize the nomination in 2028.

Former House Speaker Newt Gingrich wrote Wednesday on X that "the scale of the Republican defeat is so great that it makes the race for the GOP presidential nomination wide open." In the post, he ripped Vance for defending an ad from Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy that featured the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton. The ad received bipartisan blowback and on Tuesday, Acton defeated Ramaswamy.

"A good bit of the luster has come off the bloom," Gingrich wrote.

Bob Vander Plaats, an influential conservative leader in Iowa, where Republicans will have the first say in choosing their next nominee, predicted the losses would embolden presidential hopefuls from across the party to test the waters. By next year, he said, the field could rival the crowded 2016 Republican primary.

"There are a lot of people now who will be making the case they can take this baton and move us forward," Vander Plaats said.

A longtime Republican operative in New Hampshire, who asked not to be named, said the prospect of Vance running as a third Trump term looks increasingly "problematic" after Tuesday. The operative also expected voters in the nation's first primary will give other candidates a serious look.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, in particular, has wasted little time seizing the party's historic defeats to revive interest in his own political future. DeSantis unsuccessfully challenged Trump for the GOP nomination in 2024 and, before Tuesday, had seen his stock diminish as his time in public office came to a close.

But DeSantis in recent days has received renewed attention for his pointed critique of Trump's second stint in Washington.

In a lengthy interview with Stephen A. Smith released on the eve of the election, DeSantis accused the Trump administration of gaslighting voters, failing to tackle Washington corruption and botching its immigration rollout. He challenged Republicans to rethink their relationship with Big Tech and heed growing concerns about data centers and artificial intelligence — a notable shot at an industry that is close to Vance.

On Wednesday, DeSantis called the midterms an "extinction-level event for Republicans," while touting that Florida "was able to hold the line." Republican nominees for governor and Senate narrowly survived, but DeSantis' efforts to net his party more congressional seats via redistricting appears to have fallen short.

Several people involved in DeSantis' 2024 presidential campaign told CNN that his movements in the past 48 hours were interpreted within his orbit as keeping the door open to another White House bid. On Wednesday, DeSantis declined to discuss his future and told CNN he will "be a free man" in January.

DeSantis wasn't the only ambitious Republican rushing to rationalize the midterm losses. Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, who, said Wednesday on his popular "Verdict" podcast after his state saw massive GOP losses that "too many in politics dismissed" affordability concerns — an issue Trump himself regularly insisted was a manufactured problem.

"Understandably people were pissed off and elected Republicans didn't do enough to address their very real pain," he said.

Meanwhile, outgoing Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp, a Trump antagonist, on Wednesday laid out his own vision for the party centered on the "conservative principles of our party."

"It's time we get back to those principles in the months and years to come," Kemp wrote.

A GOP operative in neighboring South Carolina, another early-nominating state, told CNN after seeing Kemp's post: "He's running." The person noted that Kemp recently appeared in the Palmetto State to help campaign for the Republican gubernatorial candidate there, Attorney General Alan Wilson, who won on Tuesday.

To be sure, Vance remains the clear front-runner for the GOP nomination. Primary voters typically are considerably deferential to vice presidents. Vance would bring other advantages to a protracted nomination battle, including a close relationship with the party's biggest donors after serving as Republican National Committee finance chair for the past 20 months.

He also has the backing of Turning Point USA, the organization founded by the late conservative activist Charlie Kirk, that is seen as a turnkey political operation for Vance if he wants it. However, the group's political influence took a hit in the midterms as well. Republicans suffered heavy losses in states where the group is especially active, and it went all-in on Republican Andy Biggs, who is on track to the lose the Arizona governor race by double digits. A spokesman for Turning Point didn't return a request for comment.

Vance presumably would run with Trump's support — an endorsement Vance recently said he expects to receive but has yet to come. Trump does not appear especially eager to pass the torch and has at times floated other names as potential successors, most notably Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

The former Florida senator remains of favorite of many establishment figures in the GOP and has created new fans among the MAGA faithful, but it's not clear that he wants to run and has said in the past he wouldn't go up against Vance. As a key player in Trump's administration, especially on foreign policy, Rubio could face similar headwinds as Vance running to succeed him.

Despite his platform-like statement Wednesday, it isn't a sure thing that Vance will seek the nomination either. Vance himself has said he would wait until after the midterms to make that decision and close allies have publicly and privately suggested that Tuesday's outcome is likely to factor into that calculus.

Trump said Wednesday he remains in the dark on Vance's plans.

"Maybe he won't run," Trump said as he showed off construction for his White House ballroom. "I don't know who is going to run."

If Vance ultimately forgoes a White House bid, a chaotic race to replace Trump would surely follow. Several members of Trump's own Cabinet harbor presidential ambitions – including Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth – and it's unclear they would run unless Vance decided against it. Hegseth is also facing renewed criticism from his party over the war with Iran and could face an impeachment vote in the House as soon as next week, CNN reported Wednesday .

The political movements of conservative commentator Tucker Carlson remain a source of intrigue among Republicans as well. Carlson, a close friend of Vance, remains publicly supportive of the vice president and has said he won't seek the presidency. But he has also floated the creation of a third party, and supporters like former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene have encouraged him to run.

In Iowa, as voters weighed in on the midterms, some future caucus-goers were already ready to look beyond Trump as they consider who replaces him.

"I want to get away from that idea of 'Trump Republican,' and just get back to Republican-conservative," said David McDonald, a 59-year-old meat cutter from Des Moines told CNN.

Marion, Iowa, retiree Rich Sidman acknowledged the future of the GOP will come down to how Trump fares over the next two years.

"It's all about the economy, the economy, the economy," Sidman said.

He's bullish, though, on Vance after seeing him speak during the vice president's recent campaign swing through Iowa. And if the caucuses were today, that's who Sidman would vote for.

What about DeSantis — who made Iowa a second home in 2023 as he tried to seize the party from Trump?

Sidman thought for a moment, then said: "I wouldn't mind seeing DeSantis either."

CNN's Dianne Gallagher, Betsy Klein and Patrick Svitek contributed to this report.

articles.title: HUGH HEWITT: The GOP is wounded, not dead — but recovery has to start now
articles.summary: Trump faces pressure to quickly win the battle with Iran before new Democratic majorities can interfere with his authority as commander in chief.
articles.body: The GOP isn’t dead, but it sure does look and feel that way in the harsh light of the day after Tuesday’s walloping. The myth of Rasputin is that a Russian monk who pretended to mysticism was poisoned, stabbed, shot, beaten and thrown in a river. He somehow climbed out of the drink and survived. He didn’t. Miraculous recoveries only happen in the movies, as with "Boris the Bullet Dodger" in Guy Ritchie’s beloved "Snatch," which starred Jason Statham, Brad Pitt, Benicio del Toro and Dennis Farina. CONSERVATIVES STUNNED BY 'CATASTROPHIC' MIDTERM BLUE TSUNAMI, BLAME TRUMP'S IRAN WAR, HIGH GAS PRICES If you are a Republican feeling low after Tuesday night’s nationwide wipeout, "Snatch" is a good viewing choice. If you or your boss lost, you need to have a laugh because there is no crying in baseball or politics. Wipeouts happen, and the GOP isn’t going to suddenly pull itself beaten and bruised out of the Potomac. But the Republican Party isn’t dead. It’s just beaten badly, and it will take some years to mend. A lesson from the endless rebuild of the Cleveland Browns: There aren’t any shortcuts. You need patience, and you have to build through the draft. THUNE PLANS TO RUN FOR REPUBLICAN MINORITY LEADER AFTER DEMS' MIDTERM TAKEOVER The good news: There’s a best player or 10 within every state's political leadership, and it’s up to Ohio Senator Bernie Moreno to cheer up the Senate caucus and get to work recruiting and fielding a team of GOP Senate candidates for 2028. The same must go on within the much smaller House GOP conference. It’s up to President Trump to make sure the Republican National Committee, in turn, makes sure that the process of selecting his successor nominee is wide-open and robust. Debates between would-be nominees beginning early in 2027 for an Iowa primary in January 2028, with a New Hampshire primary right behind it will be an excellent forum from which many would-be presidents can test messages and themes with the country as a whole. LIZ PEEK: THERE MAY BE A SILVER LINING IN TRUMP'S BRUTAL MIDTERM DEFEAT President Trump remains the leader of a badly banged-up party, and he’s often been a terrific cheerleader and needs to be so again. Not like the "Black Knight" in 1975’s "Monty Python and the Holy Grail" — Tuesday night wasn’t a flesh wound. President Trump will study the ugly results carefully. Disasters have their own clarity about them. No need for an autopsy when the cause of death is, well, everything. President Trump’s State of the Union early in 2027 will provide an agenda around which would-be leaders-in-waiting can rally or reject. He and his team should start to work on that immediately. It will matter a great deal. The greatness of the Republic is its wonderful resilience. The Constitution is terrifically strong, a work of genius that endures. Parties thought dead beyond recovery indeed do come back. That lesson is not ancient history. No need to recall the eclipse of the GOP after Barry Goldwater’s kamikaze presidential run in 1964, which left the GOP with just 32 senators and 140 members in the House. Really. Republicans under President Reagan lost the Senate majority in 1986 and tumbled to 45 seats. It took eight years to climb back to a majority in the Upper Chamber. The GOP lost that Senate majority again in 2006, and their hole got deeper during the financial crisis in 2008. When President Obama soared to his landslide and was sworn in in 2009, there were only 41 Republican senators in attendance and 178 GOP House members. The silver lining — and it is going to need some polishing to gleam — is that the center-right and conservatives have three cycles before the post-2030 Census national redistricting gets underway. If the ongoing counting of election results in the states brings the worst, Democrats will have "trifectas"— where a party controls the governorship and both houses of the legislature— in 21 states, the GOP will have 19, and 10 will enjoy divided government. Expect redrawing of maps in the 40 states with trifectas that have not done so already, and then wait for the mandatory line drawing in 2032 after the Census. American politics is a dance that never ends. Recovery after a political crash out can be painful, but it’s best undertaken with clear eyes about what ails the GOP body politic. Anyone with a quick remedy or a single villain isn’t comprehending the scale of the rebuke. It isn’t as bad as 2008’s, but that could follow if another Great Recession looms. The only certainty for President Trump seems to be: Win the battle with Iran and do so quickly and in such a fashion that there are no doubters about who won and how. The Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait must obviously be open to all traffic passing through them unmolested by the remnants of the Iranian terrorist regime. No more ill-conceived MOUs. President Trump is the only one who matters on the decision about whether or not to win the battle with Iran and win it quickly. If the new Democratic majorities to be seated in January arrive before the battle is over, they will do their best to interfere with President Trump’s constitutional authority as commander in chief. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP So even as he helps his party stand back up, he should pursue the conflict to success. And Republicans smarting from Tuesday night’s beatdown should keep in mind that if you have to choose between running the Congress and having the Presidency, the latter is by far the better choice. articles.title: Latino, Black, Muslim, Native: Voters chose diversity in midterm election
articles.summary: Voters reshaped the Senate and House with candidates from a diverse tapestry of racial, ethnic, religious and cultural backgrounds
articles.body:
WASHINGTON – On election night, America chose diversity.

The blue tsunami that swept Democrats back into power in Congress in the Nov. 3 midterm elections also carried to victory candidates with a diverse tapestry of racial, ethnic, religious and cultural backgrounds.

Voters reshaped the Senate by electing a Methodist minister from Kansas, a Presbyterian seminarian in Texas, a Muslim physician from Michigan, a Native American in Minnesota, and, for the first time ever, an openly gay man from New Hampshire.

Candidates make history in race, gender and faith in 2026

In the House, Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries was elected for the eighth time to represent his New York congressional district – a victory that puts him on course to become the first Black speaker in January.

And, in other firsts, voters chose Black governors in Georgia, Florida and Wisconsin , a Latino governor in California , a Latina governor in Texas , and a Native American woman as governor in New Mexico . The winner in Georgia, former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, becomes the nation's first Black female governor.

The election of candidates from such varied backgrounds comes after two years of President Donald Trump and his administration erasing diversity, equity and inclusion programs across the federal government and in private and academic institutions.

"Americans spoke loudly and clearly that we still value diversity, even if the Trump administration does not," said Shaun Harper, a University of Southern California professor who has researched and written about diversity, equity and inclusion, or DEI.

The past couple of years have been tough times for people who believe in inclusion.

On the first day of his second term, Trump set out to terminate DEI policies, programs and preferences across the federal government. He shut down DEI offices, put their workers on leave, canceled DEI training programs and took down government web pages focused on diversity.

His administration opened investigations into more than 50 universities and threatened them with funding cuts in a pressure campaign to force them to dismantle DEI programs, drop race-based scholarships and alter admissions and hiring practices.

He revoked federal civil rights and non-discrimination protections for LGBTQ+ people, barred transgender Americans from serving in the military and prohibited transgender women from participating in female sports in public schools, colleges and universities.

He ordered the National Park Service to remove the rainbow-colored Pride flag at the Stonewall National Monument , which commemorates a 1969 clash in New York City between police and LGBTQ+ bar patrons that sparked the modern gay-rights movement. The administration eventually relented and allowed the flag to be returned as part of a settlement with a coalition of nonprofit groups that sued.

While America clearly voted for diversity, "I'm not prepared to say that it's a profound shift in America's racial, ethnic, religious dynamics in some deep way. Because we just don't know," said Jennifer Hochschild, a professor of government and of African and African-American studies at Harvard.

Cultural issues still divided voters in some states.

Voters in Arizona and Nebraska approved measures to ban trans athletes from participating in school sports. Votes on similar measures in Colorado and Washington state are still being counted.

"I am a proponent of democracy, and I respect that people voted with their values – even if their values are misaligned with mine," Harper said.

Virginia voters, on the other hand, stripped a two-decade-old ban on same-sex marriage from the state constitution. Several other states repealed similar constitutional bans in recent years, following the U.S. Supreme Court's decision in 2015 that legalized same-sex marriage nationwide.

Some of the candidates who won in this week's midterms endured a vitriolic assault on their religion or beliefs.

Abdul El-Sayed, a Michigan physician who triumphed to become the first Muslim elected to the Senate, faced Islamophobic and racist attacks during the brutal campaign. Trump called him a jihadist and said Congress would need a special metal detector if he was elected.

From January through August, El-Sayed was named in more than 38,000 anti-Muslim posts on social media, according to the Center for the Study of Organized Hate, a Washington-based nonprofit.

In South Carolina, Dr. Annie Andrews endured harsh criticism from Trump to pull off one of the night's most stunning Senate upsets. Her Republican opponent, Darline Graham, running in place of her late brother Lindsey Graham , ran ads condemning her over her past comments on transgender issues, and Trump mocked her by attaching an anti-transgender slur to her name.

But when the votes were counted, the winners looked a lot like America.

Michael Collins writes about the intersection of politics and culture. A veteran reporter, he has covered the White House and Congress. Follow him on X: @mcollinsNEWS

articles.title: 'Complete Armageddon': GOP seeks path forward after midterm drubbing
articles.summary: Republicans' midterm election losses scrambled the GOP. A prominent figure cast it as an "extinction-level event" after Trump's coalition collapsed.
articles.body:
WASHINGTON – Republicans' shocking midterm election losses have left the GOP scrambling, with prominent figures in the party casting the rout as an "Armageddon" and an "extinction-level event" after President Donald Trump 's coalition collapsed.

While polls indicated Trump was in for a thumping, the scale of MAGA's defeat left his party stunned.

"If we don't change, we'll take more beatings," retiring Rep. Don Bacon, R-Nebraska, said.

A day after the election, Republicans were still sorting out the results – and what they mean for the GOP in red states and battleground districts. Democrats won Senate races in deep-red Texas, Kansas, Ohio, Iowa and South Carolina, and flipped at least 30 House seats on their way to full control of Congress.

Trump's first appearance since midterms at ballroom construction site

"This is close to an extinction-level event for Republicans in many parts of the country," Florida GOP Gov. Ron DeSantis said in a news conference after the election.

Marc Short, who was Trump's liaison to Congress during his first term, wrote on social media : "Complete Armageddon for GOP."

The dismal performance prompted immediate handwringing about where the party goes next after more than a decade of domination by Trump, who said on Nov. 4 he had no regrets about the way he approached the campaign or his closing argument.

"If I was on the ballot, we would have won," Trump insisted. "We weren't able to transfer the love to candidates."

Trump touts his White House ballroom. Democrats celebrate blue wave election

'You can only step on the people so much, and they push back'

Trump pushed the GOP to hold its first-ever midterm convention and held 30 events in roughly as many days, thrusting himself into the center of the election and urging voters to "pretend" he was on the ballot in a bid to energize his MAGA base. He dangled $5,000 checks in front of Americans, promised military projects and even handed out presidential pardons.

Demographic groups that Trump made gains with in 2024 – notably Latinos and young people – defected from the Republican Party in droves. Family Research Council president Tony Perkins said the American people signaled they wanted a course correction, referencing a fight he had with the president's team in 2024 over the official GOP agenda.

"It was a very ugly process," Perkins said.

The social conservative leader said he continued to work with the administration for the good of the country, even after it "steamrolled the platform committee."

"But I think you can only step on the people so much, and they push back. And I think the feeling that a lot of us had in that process, the resentment toward the heavy-handedness, I think the nation expressed a rejection of that last night," Perkins said.

Trump reshaped the Republican Party over the last decade, driving out dissenters and pulling together a coalition that rallied his populist message around immigration, foreign policy and the economy. It fell apart, though, amid concerns about high prices and a president who promised no new wars and subsequently attacked Iran, sending the cost of gasoline soaring.

Republican leaders have been loath to question the two-term president's approach, even as his approval rating plummeted to record lows and became a drag on GOP candidates during the midterm elections.

Trump's sweeping tariffs, aggressive deportation push, eight-month war, and other policies have generated considerable backlash, and polls showed much of his agenda is unpopular; still, it met with little GOP resistance. The breadth and depth of the rebuke voters delivered Trump could change that, however.

"If it's not an inflection point, then we are doomed to repeat the same mistakes," said GOP strategist Mike DuHaime, former political director for the Republican National Committee.

Hispanic voters swung toward Democrats by 22 points compared with 2024; voters younger than 30 swung by 36 points. Democrats made gains among voters with and without college degrees, as well as among Americans earning less than $50,000 and more than $100,000 a year.

Republicans lost at least seven Senate seats and possibly more. The Alaska Senate race has not been called, while the Mississippi Senate race, which had not been figured into even the most optimistic projections for Democrats, remains tied.

In Iowa and Texas, Republicans lost governors' mansions and House seats. Republican Julia Letlow won her Senate seat in safely red Louisiana by fewer than 2 percentage points.

Moderate Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, of Pennsylvania, and centrist Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, both of whom had survived multiple elections despite being high on Democrats' target lists, were finally defeated. In North Carolina, the losses ran so deep that even Rep. Richard Hudson, chairman of the National Republican Congressional Campaign Committee, lost reelection to Congress.

"This is the kind of thing that says to aspiring presidential candidates and others down the line, that if we get thumped in '26, that ought to tell us something about the direction we take in '28," John Bolton, who served as national security advisor during Trump's first term, said in anticipating likely GOP losses during an interview shortly before the election. "And I think the clear reading is that people have had enough of Trump."

The White House pushed back on the criticism in a defiant email.

"Every time the Radical Left, the Fake News, and the professional panic class have written President Trump's obituary, they have been wrong. They will be wrong again," it said.

It also sought to shift the attention to Democrats.

"In the final two years of his presidency, Democrats will try – and fail – to reverse everything President Trump has done," the release said, listing more than a dozen bullet points that accuse Democrats of seeking to reopen the border, raise taxes and launch impeachment probes.

Candidates make history in race, gender and faith in 2026

But Republican critics of the president worry he has done historic damage to his party that can't be untangled over the next two years.

Former Michigan Republican Rep. Fred Upton, who voted to impeach Trump and endorsed his Democratic opponent in 2024, said it will take "many cycles to remedy" what happened on Nov. 3, comparing it to what Republicans faced after President Richard Nixon resigned amid the Watergate scandal.

"I think it fractures MAGA and there'll be a lot of pieces, and we'll see who tries to put Humpty Dumpty together again," Upton said of the 2026 election.

In 1974, Democrats picked up four seats in the Senate and 49 in the House. A net 34 seats have been won by Democrats in this year's midterms so far.

Moving away from Trump could be difficult, though. The president still has the bully pulpit and plenty of hardcore fans.

He was able to oust four-term Texas Sen. John Cornyn and two-term Louisiana Sen. Bill Cassidy in favor of his preferred candidates in this year's Republican primaries. While 38% of likely voters in battleground states strongly or somewhat approved of his job performance in a New York Times/Siena poll released two days before the midterms, that number was 82% among Republicans.

Donald Trump's second term: Actions, travels of the 47th president

The immediate loser could be Vice President JD Vance, if he moves forward with an anticipated bid for president.

In a more than 600-word statement on the outcome of the election, Vance said he was told in the lead-up to the election that Trump-Vance 2024 supporters were angry and planning to vote for the other party.

"Undoubtedly there were places we could have done better on turnout. But the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026," the vice president said.

Vance said there would be quite a bit of "infighting and arguing over what happened and why," including over their economic messaging. "But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone."

"Any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there," Vance said.

Former GOP Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, one of Trump's most ardent supporters in Congress before resigning from office and becoming one of his chief critics, responded to Vance's comments on social media , saying Republicans lost because the administration didn't deliver on its campaign promises.

"Blaming the Iran war won't work, and it's not going to be an easy pivot," Greene said.
