articles.title: Congress defeat: How Trump’s allies are distancing themselves from Iran war
articles.summary: US Vice President JD Vance blames the war for the midterm rout as Democrats prepare to use Congress to rein it in.
articles.body:
Vice President JD Vance has blamed the war on Iran for the Republican Party’s sweeping defeat in Tuesday’s midterm elections , in which Democrats won control of both chambers of the United States Congress.

“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance wrote in a lengthy post on X on Wednesday.

Senator Ted Cruz, a longtime Iran hawk, also turned on the conflict, saying in an episode of his podcast on Wednesday that it “should have been brief, decisive, and over”.

This week, President Donald Trump has insisted that he has no regrets. “I did the right thing. I would have done it again,” he told The Wall Street Journal about launching a war on Iran alongside Israel in February.

So, why are Trump’s allies breaking ranks, and what does it mean for the war? Here’s what you need to know:

Vance, a likely 2028 presidential candidate and heir apparent to Trump’s Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement, questioned whether the war had been worth the political cost.

“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so,” he wrote.

Citing an unnamed pollster, Vance said ending the Iran war and “changing our relationship with Israel” were two of the top four answers given ahead of this week’s midterms by Americans who voted for Trump in 2024 but planned to vote for Democrats this year.

Cruz’s criticism came from another direction. The war had “dragged on too long”, he said in a post on X, adding that Washington “should never, under any circumstances, give the Ayatollah billions of dollars”.

He was apparently referring to the June memorandum of understanding signed by Washington and Tehran, which included a $300bn fund to help rebuild post-war Iran among several topics for discussion in wider peace talks. The proposal for the fund triggered hefty pushback from conservative lawmakers, including Cruz, who said it amounted to a massive payout for the Iranian regime.

The June agreement, which provided for a ceasefire at the time, quickly fell apart , however.

Trump told reporters at the White House on Wednesday that Vance’s assessment was “largely true”, blaming higher fuel prices, as a result of the war, for Americans turning against his party. But the president insisted the war was necessary to stop Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.

Republicans are positioning themselves for the 2028 presidential election, which Trump will not be able to run in, as he will have served the maximum of two terms as president.

Paul Musgrave, associate professor of government at Georgetown University in Qatar, told Al Jazeera there are “major internal divisions within the Republican Party” over the war.

The US decision to attack Iran triggered a global fuel crisis with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which has cost the US taxpayer an estimated $47bn so far . This means candidates for 2028 likely need to distance themselves from the war if they have any hope of winning.

But Musgrave said hawks such as Cruz and the late Senator Lindsey Graham had, in fact, long pushed for a war on Iran. Now that they have one, “it has been a disaster internationally and domestically for them”, he said, but “they can’t walk away”. Instead, they are limited to criticising its length and execution.

Vance, however, “is trying to represent a more isolationist wing of the Republican Party, and is willing to walk away from the war and probably other commitments to win favour with a large part of the Trump base”, Musgrave said. “This is all about positioning for 2028 and the future of the Republican Party.”

Natasha Lindstaedt, a professor at the Department of Government at the University of Essex, told Al Jazeera: “JD Vance was never in favour of the Iran war to begin with, and he was put in a really awkward position of trying to negotiate the end of the Iran war when he himself didn’t want the US to get involved in that war in the first place.”

“It just wasn’t a natural fit for him, and now his true colours are coming out a little bit here. And he’s willing to break from Trump,” she said. “Maybe he sees the writing is on the wall.”

Lindstaedt said other Republicans may be finally realising that this is the point where they need to separate themselves from the Trump brand because it is not helping them.

John Feehery, a former Republican congressional staffer, told Al Jazeera the Iran war “was a big part” of the defeat, alongside energy prices, healthcare and corruption. The race to succeed Trump has already begun, he said, pointing to Vance and Florida Governor Ron DeSantis.

What can Democrats do to make the most of this?

Limit the money available for continuing the war, and squeeze the people running it.

Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said on Wednesday that “this war must end”, pointing to Congress’s control of funding.

“The Founding Fathers had the power of the purse as one of the ways of deterring a president who does war without the consent of the American people,” he told a news conference in Washington, DC.

Congressman Ro Khanna proposed a continuing resolution “prohibiting the financing of any combat activities of the US military in Iran”, ending the war “like we did for Vietnam”.

Musgrave said appropriations would be “a principal lever”, especially given “the havoc that has been wreaked with the defence budget by the spiralling expenses of the war in Iran”.

Feehery, meanwhile, noted that the defence budget and an extension of the debt limit would both need bipartisan support to pass.

Official hearings and investigations, over which Democrats now wield a great deal more power by dominating both chambers of Congress, could also “make the war unpopular and harass or drive from office several key players”, Musgrave said.

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth is also in the firing line. Outgoing Republican Senator Thom Tillis told CBS News that Hegseth would face a “reckoning” for his part in the Iran war, while Democratic Representative Jason Crow labelled the defence chief as “incompetent and corrupt”.

But Musgrave warned that the bigger fight will likely be over the Trump administration’s refusal to obey congressional spending limits. “I expect many more fights over that than even over the War Powers Act ,” he said, referring to the law that requires presidents to gain Congress’s permission before launching a war overseas, but which many presidents have managed to circumvent in the past.

Yes, even as diplomatic efforts and Qatar-led mediated talks continue.

On Tuesday, as Americans voted, US forces struck Iran’s Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, the first attack there since June. US officials described the strikes as “defensive”.

US media, citing officials, also reported that the military’s Central Command had prepared for strikes that could begin as early as Wednesday, when three US aircraft carriers would be in the region.

Giorgio Cafiero, CEO of Gulf State Analytics, said Trump “prides himself in leaving everyone, including the Iranians, constantly guessing”.

With the midterms behind him, “Trump may conclude that he has nothing to lose and choose to significantly escalate this crisis”, Cafiero told Al Jazeera.

Democrats “won’t even take power until January 2027”, he noted. “So perhaps Trump will see these upcoming months as a window of opportunity to act very aggressively toward Tehran.”

Tehran has already promised to respond to any attacks.

Majed al-Ansari, a spokesperson for Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said Washington and Tehran “remain committed to the negotiation process”, though Iran called the latest US response to Tehran’s conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz “unconvincing”.

Cafiero said Doha’s mediation “can only prove successful if a willingness to compromise on core issues exists on both sides”. He added: “Israel will do all it can to play spoiler to any diplomatic arrangement that Qatar may ultimately help facilitate.”

Trump told The Financial Times on election night that he had no immediate plans to order new attacks.

articles.title: Sílvia Orriols: "La huelga general es una españolada, no nos incumbe"
articles.standfirst: La líder de Aliança Catalana critica la convocatoria para el 11 de noviembre
articles.summary: La líder de Aliança Catalana critica la convocatoria para el 11 de noviembre
articles.body: La líder de Aliança Catalana, Sílvia Orriols, se ha desvinculado completamente de la huelga general convocado para el próximo miércoles 11 de noviembre. "Nosotros pensamos que esta vaga es directamente una españolada, por lo tanto no nos incumbe. Y que además tiene una connotación claramente política", ha comentado durante una entrevista a TV3. Sílvia Orriols ha argumentado su posicionamiento. "La movilizan aquellos sindicatos que están patrocinados y subvenciones por los partidos de izquierdas españoles, precisamente justo antes de las elecciones", comentado. La dirigente política ha explicado que la meta de la huelga general convocada para el próximo 11 de noviembre. "Es para condicionar el voto de los ciudadanos. Por lo tanto, no consideramos que debamos unirnos a este tipo de teatros", ha reflexionado. Sílvia Orriols ha desvelado qué hará en los próximos comicios del 29 de noviembre. "Yo me abstendré, porque nunca he votado en unas elecciones españolas al no ser española. Por lo tanto, me gustaría que hubiera una fuerte abstención en Cataluña que reivindicara precisamente esta voluntad de reconvertirnos en el estado que un día fuimos", ha comentado durante la entrevista en la televisión autonómica catalana. "Cada votante es una persona libre que bajo su criterio y su sensibilidad emitirá el voto que crea conveniente o dejará de votar si tiene la misma percepción o sensibilidad que yo. Pero en ningún caso estoy recomendando ni estoy dando instrucciones ni manifestando voluntades", ha insistido la líder de Aliança Catalana, con un peso electoral cada vez mayor en Cataluña según los recientes sondeos. Por otra parte, Sílvia Orriols ha descartado que el hecho de no presentarse a las elecciones generales suponga un impulso a VOX: "Trabajamos únicamente por los catalanes y por Cataluña y evidentemente no para ninguna otra formación política. Y todavía menos para una que pretende la subordinación total de nuestra nación".

articles.title: Healthcare powers Democrats’ midterm rout: 4 takeaways
articles.summary: Voters offered a strong rebuke of the GOP health agenda on Tuesday night as Democrats took control of both chambers of Congress, with voters largely rejectin...
articles.body:
Voters offered a strong rebuke of the GOP health agenda on Tuesday night as Democrats took control of both chambers of Congress, with voters largely rejecting Republicans who pushed sweeping healthcare cuts .

Here are four takeaways from the results.

Health affordability was a winning message

Democratic candidates made healthcare affordability a key part of their messaging. They campaigned on restoring the enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies and on delaying or rolling back the Medicaid cuts passed under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

Polling over the past year consistently showed that voters are worried about the cost of healthcare — and trusted Democrats more to fix it. Democrats leaned into that message, and the results were borne out on Tuesday.

Ohio pediatrician and Gov.-elect Amy Acton (D), who led the state's COVID-19 response, kept healthcare costs top of mind throughout her campaign.

She prioritized issues like forgiving medical debt, ending surprise billing and keeping Medicaid accessible.

"There is no more breathing room. From the grocery and gas bills, to the utilities, to childcare, to healthcare costs, Ohioans are doing everything right, but they just can't get ahead," Acton said in her victory speech.

Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, an epidemiologist and former public health director of Detroit and Wayne County, made single-payer healthcare and a guarantee of care a central part of his campaign for Senate in Michigan.

"America's greatness is the fight to guarantee all of us the healthcare we need if we get sick," El-Sayed told his supporters during a victory speech late Tuesday night.

Democratic doctors and scientists rebuff RFK Jr.

Voters across the country chose physicians who ran diametrically against the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) agenda and the Trump administration's health policies.

Dr. Annie Andrews (D) in South Carolina made it known early on that her decision to run for office was spurred by the nomination of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to his role. Andrews has pledged to "lead the charge" to impeach and remove Kennedy.

"I've watched as insurance companies stood between sick children and the care that they need. I've seen how decisions made in Washington affect the lives of the children and families I've cared for, and that's why I decided to run, because I believe we have a responsibility to leave our children something better than what we inherited," Andrews said in her victory speech.

With El-Sayed and Andrews winning their respective races, the Senate will have Democratic doctors for the first time since former Sen. Ernest H. Gruening (D-Alaska) left office in 1969. And Andrews will be the first Democratic practicing physician in the upper chamber in nearly 90 years.

In the House, California pediatrician Richard Pan managed to flip the state's 6th Congressional District and unseat incumbent Rep. Kevin Kiley (I). Pan ran on a campaign of holding the administration accountable for its healthcare policies.

The blue medical wave on Tuesday night was also a victory for 314 Action, the political action committee dedicated to getting Democrats in STEM elected.

"314 Action candidates flipped the House because this was a healthcare election, and we elect outsiders who voters trust," 314 Action President Shaughnessy Naughton said in a statement. "Millions of Americans lost healthcare because of Trump, RFK Jr. and Republicans in Congress, and on Tuesday — voters answered by electing a new wave of doctors and scientists to Washington. This proves that STEM candidates are better positioned than any other candidate to win battleground races."

Democrats will have major decisions ahead on healthcare, and party leaders will need to navigate the divisions between progressive factions that are itching to pursue "Medicare for All" and moderates who want more incremental change.

Buoyed by the victory of candidates like El-Sayed in Michigan, progressives in the House and Senate are expected to make a significant push for single-payer healthcare.

"WHO WANTS MEDICARE FOR ALL?" Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.), who won reelection, wrote on the social platform X late Tuesday.

During his victory speech Tuesday night, El-Sayed thanked his supporters in a call-and-response chant for backing "money out of politics, money in your pocket, and Medicare for All."

While major change is unlikely in the next two years with President Trump still in office, advocates are looking to set the agenda with an eye toward the 2028 presidential election.

Neither House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) nor Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) — the likely Speaker and Senate majority leader, respectively — has endorsed the most recent version of Medicare for All.

But letting a bill come to the floor during the Trump presidency would catapult Medicare for All directly into the 2028 conversation and show Democrats no longer fear attacks about taking away people's private insurance.

As many adults and families struggle to afford health costs, the popularity of Medicare for All is growing. A KFF poll in September showed two-thirds of Americans favored a "single government plan."

A national debate would likely include more details about costs and trade-offs that aren't being captured in surface-level campaign slogans.

The same poll showed support plummeted when people heard the arguments that Medicare for All could lead to delays in medical tests and treatments and tax increases or threaten the current Medicare program.

But support grew when respondents heard that a national insurance plan could make health insurance "a right" or eliminate premiums and cost-sharing.

The alliance between supporters of Kennedy's MAHA movement and Trump-aligned Republicans was already fraying in the run-up to Tuesday.

The results show that alliance may be on life support.

Conservatives and the Trump administration "broke almost every promise on MAHA, no new wars, Epstein, affordability… There is a clear direction of where conservatives need to head in 2028 if we want a fighting chance. Otherwise AOC will be president," Turning Point USA commentator Alex Voetberg wrote on X late Tuesday.

Major MAHA-aligned Republican politicians in Iowa, Texas and Kansas lost, dealing a major blow to Kennedy and his allies in the movement.

The most significant defeat for Kennedy and the vaccine-skeptic wing of the MAHA movement came when Iowa GOP gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn lost in a landslide to Democrat Rob Sand.

Kennedy and MAHA groups invested significant time and money promoting Lahn, who vowed to ban COVID-19 vaccines, end school vaccine mandates, clean Iowa's water and regulate chemicals if elected.

During a MAHA rally late last week, Kennedy called Lahn's race "the most important election going on in this country."

Yet Sand also leaned into the environmental wing of MAHA and made tackling the environmental causes of cancer — and blaming "Big Ag" — a key part of his platform.

Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall (R) lost his race in a major upset to Democrat Adam Hamilton. Marshall, chair of the Senate's MAHA Caucus and a senior member of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, has been key to shepherding Trump's health nominees through Congress and giving MAHA priorities a legislative voice.

While some MAHA grassroots activists think the movement's key principles should be nonpartisan, its leaders have aligned themselves with Trump and parts of the Republican Party. There have been months of infighting over the movement's campaign strategy.

In his concession speech, Lahn said MAHA is a "real movement that has legs."

"That says that corporate interests, lobbyists, career politicians, that we are putting them on notice tonight because the movement is just beginning here and now."

articles.title: Visualising how the US midterms turned the map blue
articles.summary: Who voted, which seats flipped and who made history? A look at the numbers behind the 2026 US midterm elections.
articles.body:
A Democratic wave swept the United States Congress as Americans turned out in near-record numbers to strip President Donald Trump’s Republicans of their majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate.

About 122.7 million ballots have already been counted in the November 3 midterm elections , according to preliminary estimates from the University of Florida’s Election Lab. About 48.8 percent of the eligible population voted, the second-highest midterm turnout in more than a century, just below 2018.

In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera maps the seats Democrats flipped, charts turnout across the country, and looks at the history made on election night.

Votes are still being counted, but as of 09:00 GMT on Thursday, November 5, Democrats have won at least 240 seats in the House and 54 in the Senate, enough to control both chambers. Republicans have won 147 House seats and 44 in the Senate.

Forty-eight House races and two Senate races, in Alaska and Mississippi, have yet to be called. Democrats could end up with more than 260 seats in the House and 56 in the Senate.

The widget below shows the latest results as they come in. Visit this page for full live results.

Of about 210 million registered voters, 54.5 million had already cast their ballots early by 10am US East Coast time (15:00 GMT) on Sunday, November 1, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab. About 30 million voted in person and 24 million by mail.

By the time polls closed on Tuesday, the total had more than doubled. The Election Lab estimates that 122.7 million ballots have been tallied, with 48.76 percent of eligible voters casting a ballot.

Turnout varied widely by state. Maine recorded the highest, with 65.78 percent of eligible voters casting a ballot, followed by Minnesota (65.16 percent) and Michigan (63.65 percent). West Virginia had the lowest, at 33.33 percent, followed by Oklahoma (37.08 percent) and Hawaii (37.68 percent).

The map below shows voter turnout by state.

Democrats needed a net gain of four Senate seats to reach 51, the number needed for a majority, because Vice President JD Vance can break a 50-50 tie in Republicans’ favour.

They went well beyond that, flipping seven Republican-held seats and securing at least 54 seats in the incoming Senate.

James Talarico won in Texas, Roy Cooper in North Carolina, Annie Andrews in South Carolina, Sherrod Brown in Ohio, Josh Turek in Iowa, and Adam Hamilton in Kansas. In Maine, Democrats unseated Susan Collins.

Democrats also held onto all their existing seats, even when they had a new candidate, like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan.

In the 435-member House, the target was 218 seats for a majority.

Democrats crossed that threshold with ease, flipping at least 31 Republican-held districts across the country, including in areas reshaped by new congressional maps. The gains came both in closely contested districts and in places where Democratic victories were less expected.

In New York’s 17th congressional district, Cait Conley defeated Mike Lawler, and in New Jersey’s 7th, Rebecca Bennett unseated Thomas Kean Jr. In Virginia’s 2nd, Elaine Luria defeated Jen Kiggans, while in Wisconsin’s 3rd, Rebecca Cooke defeated Derrick Van Orden. In Michigan’s 4th, Democrat Sean McCann defeated Bill Huizenga, an eight-term incumbent.

In Texas, Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton, giving the state its first Democratic senator since 1993. Gina Hinojosa also unseated Republican Governor Greg Abbott, becoming the state’s first Latina governor, and its first Democratic governor since 1994.

The breakthroughs reached well beyond Texas. Kansas elected its first Democratic senator since 1932, and South Carolina will have its first since 2005.

Democrats also flipped seats in Iowa, Maine, North Carolina and Ohio. Together, the wins broke through Republican strongholds across the South and Midwest, stripping Trump’s party of its Senate majority with two years of his term remaining.

Several other candidates also made history :

Michigan : Abdul El-Sayed became the first Muslim elected to the US Senate.

New Hampshire : Chris Pappas became the first openly gay man elected to the Senate.

Georgia : Keisha Lance Bottoms, the great-great-granddaughter of a slave, became the first Black woman elected governor of a US state.

New Mexico : Deb Haaland became the first Native American woman elected governor.

US House : Hakeem Jeffries could become the first Black speaker of the House if the chamber elects him in January.

The new Congress takes office on January 3, 2027. Until then, Republicans keep control of both chambers.

articles.title: ‘A beautifully American story’: El-Sayed's historic Senate victory resonates with Muslim Americans
articles.summary: (AP) — Campaigning relentlessly across Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed didn’t highlight the possibility that he could become the first Muslim elected to the U. But...
articles.body:
DEARBORN, Mich. (AP) — Campaigning relentlessly across Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed didn't highlight the possibility that he could become the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. But with victory in hand , he savored his triumph over the vitriol aimed at him and his fellow Muslim Americans.

"They tried to demonize people because of how they pray," he told The Associated Press on Wednesday. "And Michigan — the whole Michigan — clapped back. People don't want that. They're sick of it."

He showed his pride in his victory speech, declaring: "My name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed."

Twenty-five years after the Sept. 11 attacks and their aftermath yanked anti-Muslim sentiment into the forefront of American life, those emotions are shared by many Muslim Americans in Michigan and across the country.

They saw a surge of anti-Muslim rhetoric after Zohran Mamdani's election as New York City mayor a year ago, and they saw the attacks intensify as El-Sayed became the new prime target. President Donald Trump called him a "jihadist" who was "on the side of the terrorists." Dozens of Trump's fellow Republicans in Congress formed a Sharia-Free America Caucus, depicting Islam's religious code as a threat to the U.S. Constitution.

But now, after El-Sayed's defeat of GOP rival Mike Rogers was confirmed early Wednesday, there is a pervasive sense that a broader victory is at hand.

The outcome "represents a historic turning point for American Muslim political engagement and a historic defeat for the politics of hate," said Nihad Awad, national executive director of the Council on American-Islamic Relations.

"Anti-Muslim extremists, Israel lobby groups and even the president of the United States used every smear in the book to paint Dr. El-Sayed as a Muslim boogeyman," he said. "None of it was true, and none of it worked. Anti-Muslim hate was on the ballot, and it failed."

In Dearborn, talk of 'a beautifully American story'

Excitement over El-Sayed's victory was palpable in Dearborn, a city near Detroit with a sizable Arab American population. The mayor, Abdullah Hammoud, said residents showed up at the ballot box in huge numbers.

"What a beautifully American story," Hammoud said. "One of our brightest and best earned the support of the majority of Michiganders who participated in yesterday's election. And regardless of the direction in which he prays, they're sending him to the U.S. Senate."

Hammoud, who has known El-Sayed for more than a decade, said although his win was important for many Arab Americans, people voted for him because of his platform, not his identity. He cited support in Dearborn for independent Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders' 2016 presidential campaign . Sanders, who is Jewish and caucuses with Democrats, ran on a progressive platform.

In El-Sayed, residents of Dearborn "finally saw themselves and a candidate who appealed to them, but it had to do with far more than just his ethnicity or his religion," Hammoud said. "It was honestly because of the policies and building a coalition with this community in an honest way."

When Zaynah Jadallah, 26, canvassed for El-Sayed in Dearborn, she said most people told her they already planned on voting for him before inviting her in for water or food. She credited the name recognition to El-Sayed's grassroots campaigning and his pride in his Egyptian heritage.

"He's always been proud of his identity. He never shied away from it or from saying his name," Jadallah said.

Yasmin El-Sayed, no relation to the senator-elect, took her two daughters to the Detroit watch party from New York. She teared up after the victory speech.

"Having grown up in a post-9/11 world, being Muslim, being Arab myself, never in a million years did I think we would see what we saw today," she said.

In a time of suspicion of government, a message of representation

El-Sayed depicted his election as a victory for all those "who don't see themselves reflected in our government or who've been told that they don't belong for some reason or another — not just how they pray but who they love, how they identify, the color of their skin, where they grew up.″

"I didn't run to be the first Muslim senator. I ran to be the next senator of the state of Michigan who happens to be Muslim," he said. ″But I also know that democracy is constantly about the conversation about who we are, who we want to be."

"Michigan proved just how big we are. Rejected a hateful, spiteful campaign that had nothing to say about the issues and only wanted to point to my name and my face," he added. ″I want all of those folks out there who have been told that America's not big enough for them to reflect on that. America really is big enough for all of us."

Mohamed Gula, CEO of the Muslim American advocacy group Emgage Action, said he was elated by El-Sayed's triumph after a year of "extremely Islamophobic and disgusting rhetoric being used as a campaign strategy."

"For Abdul to come out last night and use his full name meant the world to someone who grew up in post-9/11 America, where the Muslim American community was seen through a national security lens," Gula said.

"Our children, years from now, will be able to run for office," he said, "to be seen as who they are."

A debate over the place of Sharia law — and its very definition

Among the most frequent targets of anti-Muslim rhetoric was Sharia, the religious code that provides Muslims with guidance on how to lead righteous lives. At the Republicans' midterm convention in Dallas, some of the loudest cheers came after GOP Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas declared: "Sharia law has no place in America."

Muslim American civic leaders and scholars — in Texas and other states — responded forcefully to the anti-Sharia rhetoric that dates back more than 15 years .

They passionately defended Sharia — the way it's practiced in the United States — as positive guidance that shares elements with the codes of other faiths, such as the Ten Commandments and the collective body of Jewish law derived from the Torah. They rebutted the claims of GOP critics that Sharia is a coercive code that threatens the Constitution and the judicial system.

Gula noted that Republican Texas Gov. Greg Abbott and Attorney General Ken Paxton were among the leaders of the anti-Sharia campaign. Abbott lost his bid for reelection in Tuesday's voting, and Paxton was trounced by Democrat James Talarico in the race for a U.S. Senate seat.

"I saw this as not just Muslims standing against Islamophobia as never before," Gula said. "I saw Americans saying hate will not be used as a campaign issue ... we are not going to accept hate."

Asma Uddin, a professor at Michigan State University's College of Law, has argued that many American politicians are depicting ordinary Muslim religious practices — such as prayer, choice of apparel, family counseling and mosque attendance — as evidence of political danger.

"What I find especially exciting is that El-Sayed won in a political climate where being visibly Muslim can still be a liability," she said. His victory "gives us real reason for optimism. It suggests that anti-Muslim attacks don't necessarily carry the political weight that those deploying them assume they do."

Cappelletti reported from Washington and Crary from New York.

articles.title: Midterm results live updates: Alaska, Mississippi Senate races still neck-and-neck
articles.summary: Democrats have won control of Congress, but the midterms aren't over. Follow live updates on the key races still to be decided.
articles.body:
Republicans are still licking their political wounds after Democrats' resounding midterm election wins on Tuesday.

The seismic blue wave left the GOP scrambling and eyeing a path forward for a post-Trump era, even as the president remains at the helm of the party — and White House — for the next two years.

"If we don't change, we'll take more beatings," retiring Rep. Don Bacon, R-Nebraska, said.

Democrats, meanwhile, are continuing to celebrate resounding midterm election wins over President Trump , while hoping to add to their congressional majorities as the final races are decided.

"The biggest takeaway from last night is that millions of voters put their faith in Democrats to fight for them," Democratic Party Chairman Ken Martin said Wednesday in the wake of the stunning cross-country electoral rout. "Now, we're going to get to work and fight for a more affordable America."

A previously listless Democratic Party flipped the House, Senate and pulled off several down-ballot races, from protecting abortion rights in some states to winning the governor's office in Texas. As of early Thursday, Democrats had flipped seven Senate seats and more than 30 House seats. Votes are still being counted in the U.S. Senate races in Alaska and Mississippi , as well as dozens of House contests.

Trump said he will accept the midterm results and work with Democrats, but he also pledged to veto Democratic bills that come across his desk.

He called the veto the "ultimate power," though Congress can override a presidential veto with a two-thirds vote in both chambers.

Byron Donalds celebrates historic victory as Florida’s first Black governor

House Oversight Committee lays out 2027 plans

11:10 AM ET, November 5 2026, Sarah D. Wire

The incoming House Oversight Committee chairman Rep. Robert Garcia of California outlined the four main investigations that Democrats will be opening when they take back the house in January.

"We should be very clear that the American people have spoken loudly and clearly - they want change," Garcia told reporters during a news conference in Huntington Beach Wednesday. "They are tired of the destruction and the corruption of Donald Trump and this administration."

Garcia called Democrats' electoral victories nationwide a mandate.

Garcia said that the committee will be "laser focused" on: the Trump family's financial gains during President Donald Trump's time in office; the Department of Homeland Security and ICE's immigration enforcement efforts; corporate corruption and Jeffrey Epstein and who was involved.

Gingrich calls GOP race for president 'wide open' with 'bloom' off VP JD Vance

11:06 AM ET, November 5 2026, Bart Jansen

Newt Gingrich, an adviser to the Trump administration's Pentagon and a former Republican House speaker, called "the race for the GOP presidential wide open" after Democrats swept into control of Congress.

Gingrich said Vice President JD Vance would have had a claim on the nomination if Republicans had done well, but "the luster has come off the bloom" because of his "go-slow strategy blowing up in Iran" and his support for an Ohio gubernatorial ad that featured a mother attacking her own daughter.

"The number of people who want to draft Secretary of State Marco Rubio is staggering," Gingrich said in a social media post . "In addition, Ted Cruz, Tom Cotton, Ron DeSantis, Pete Hegseth, Glenn Youngkin, and a surprising number of people may decide this is their chance to take advantage of the chaos of the shocking defeat and seek to be the champion who can rescue the party and the country."

11:02 AM ET, November 5 2026, Zachary Schermele

Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert still has yet to learn whether or not she will secure a fourth term in Congress, as votes are still being counted in a tight race in Colorado's 4th Congressional District.

Boebert, a onetime staunch MAGA ally who has at times notably strayed from President Trump , is facing Democrat Eileen Laubacher. By NBC News' count , Laubacher was up by only a couple thousand votes just before noon ET Thursday, with roughly 93% of the vote in. Thousands more ballots are left to count.

El-Sayed keeps invoking Michigan-Ohio State rivalry

10:43 AM ET, November 5 2026, Erin Mansfield

Continuing a theme from the campaign trail, Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed once again invoked the college football rivalry between the University of Michigan, which he attended, and The Ohio State University, the alma mater of Republican Vice President JD Vance.

"I just pointed out the fact that constitutionally he's obligated to swear me in," El-Sayed, a Democrat, told CNN about Vance's role as the president of the U.S. Senate.

"And he did go to Ohio State University, which of course is a lesser university than the University of Michigan," El-Sayed quipped. "I'm just, I'm stating facts."

Data center, AI stocks fall after Democratic sweep of Congress

10:42 AM ET, November 5 2026, Bart Jansen

Stocks related to data centers and the development of artificial intelligence are down after Democrats regaining control of Congress sparked concerns about industry expansion.

Data centers were a potent political message in state and local elections, although not entirely along partisan lines. Advocates such as President Donald Trump argued that development of data centers is an economic benefit. But critics including many Democrats contend data centers drive up electricity costs and consume large amounts of water to cool equipment.

Stock prices fell Nov. 5 in companies such as CoreWeave, down 3%, and Nebius, down 6%.

"The market's moving from the promise of AI to the price of AI," said Ted Parkhill, CEO of Incline Investment Management.

Abdul El-Sayed says he'll work in Senate with GOP rivals such as Ted Cruz

10:25 AM ET, November 5 2026, Bart Jansen

Democratic Senator-elect Adbul El-Sayed of Michigan, who will be the first Muslim in the Senate, said he would work with Republicans who said the harshest things about him, including alleging he was a national security risk, such as Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas.

"Ted Cruz said some awful things," El-Sayed said on MS NOW's "Morning Joe." "I will sit down with Ted Cruz, and if he's got a bill that makes sense to get money out of politics, put money in pockets, pass Medicare for all, I'll work with him on it, so long as he's willing to do it in good faith."

GOP Sen. Cruz blames election losses on high cost of living, including tariffs

10:23 AM ET, November 5 2026, Bart Jansen

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, called the Democratic wave in the midterm elections a "blue tsunami" and an "ass kicking" that Republicans will have to reckon with.

Texans hadn't elected a Democrat to statewide office since 1994, yet Democrats swept the posts on Nov. 3. Cruz said Republicans showed up at the polls but that they didn't like the candidates – and he took aim at issues Demcorats raised against Trump, including tariffs and allegations of corruption.

In Kansas, for example, which elected its first Democratic senator since 1932, nearly one-third of voters listed the cost of living as their No. 1 concern. That was followed by corruption, the Iran war terrible candidates and the trade war with Canada.

"Food is too high, gas is too high, diesel is too high, insurance is too high, life is too high," Cruz said in a social media post . "Tariffs have made everything too expensive, and the Iran war has dragged on too long."

Latino, Black, Muslim, Native: Voters chose diversity in midterm election

07:17 AM ET, November 5 2026, Michael Collins

WASHINGTON – On election night, America chose diversity .

The blue tsunami that swept Democrats back into power in the House and Senate in the Nov. 3 midterm elections carried to victory candidates with a diverse tapestry of racial, ethnic, religious and cultural backgrounds.

Voters reshaped the Senate by electing a Methodist minister from Kansas, a Presbyterian seminarian in Texas, a Muslim physician from Michigan, a Native American in Minnesota, and, for the first time ever, an openly gay man from New Hampshire. Read more .

Mississippi Senate race outcome might take days

07:06 AM ET, November 5 2026, Michael Loria

It remains unclear who Mississippi will send to the U.S. Senate, and the state's top elections official is warning the final result might not be known for days.

"Counties have 10 days from the date of the election to submit their certified results to our office, which is November 13," Secretary of State Michael Watson said in a statement Wednesday. "Additionally, there are approximately 3,600 outstanding absentee-by-mail ballots that must be received within five business days and an unknown number of affidavit ballots that will be processed within the 10-day window counties have to certify their results."

On the ballot in the Magnolia State are Republican incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democratic challenger Scott Colom. With 80% of ballots counted, Colom held a slight edge, with 353,440 votes to Hyde-Smith's 352,203. Independent Ty Pinkins had 15,696 votes, USA TODAY previously reported.

The tight race could deliver Democrats an eighth flipped Senate seat and make Colom Mississippi's first Democratic U.S. senator since Sen. John C. Stennis left office in 1989. Hyde-Smith has held the seat since 2018.

Where does the Alaska Senate race stand?

06:51 AM ET, November 5 2026, James Powel and Aysha Bagchi

In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola leads incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan by 637 votes with 74% of ballots counted, according to the Associated Press . Peltola and Sullivan are both below the 50% threshold needed to avoid sending the race to Alaska's ranked-choice voting system .

Alaska's voting system can make results take longer to determine in close races. According to David Becker, a former Justice Department voting rights lawyer who runs the Center for Election Innovation & Research, election officials will have to wait "for some time" for votes to come in from remote areas.

The state also has a significant population of military voters, whose ballots can arrive up to 15 days after Election Day, as long as they were postmarked by Election Day.

If no candidate gets more than 50% of the vote, the state's ranked choice voting system comes into play, which could mean further delays. Under state law, the ranked choice tally wouldn't start until Nov. 18.

"So it might be the second half of November where we get a really good sense of that," Becker said.

articles.title: DeSantis: ‘No question’ midterms a ‘rebuke’ of Trump, Congress
articles.summary: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) cast blame on Congress and President Trump after Republicans suffered significant losses in the midterm elections. “This midter...
articles.body:
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) cast blame on Congress and President Trump after Republicans suffered significant losses in the midterm elections.

"This midterm, no question, was a rebuke of the president and the Congress by Democrats, independents and some Republicans that crossed over," he told Fox News's Laura Ingraham.

"But a lot of our voters who stayed home, they stayed home because they were frustrated with the lack of productivity from Republicans in the House and Senate," the governor continued. "That's just a fact. They were promised big things, and they didn't deliver it."

Exit polling from Tuesday indicated that economic issues were the central motivating factor for many voters in this election, with 75 percent of voters in a CBS News poll saying the condition of the U.S. economy was "not good."

An analysis by The New York Times , looking at nationwide exit surveys, found that voters from every demographic moved toward favoring Democratic candidates in this election from 2024.

The Democratic Party secured notable victories in red states like Texas, Kansas and South Carolina and flipped control of both chambers of Congress, results that have been labeled a " blue tsunami ."

In DeSantis's Florida, Democrats gained ground in state races and defeated GOP candidates for House seats, although Republicans maintained control of other major statewide offices.

The GOP issued their own analysis of what went wrong in Tuesday's election. Texas Sens. John Cornyn (R) and Ted Cruz (R) responded to the historic defeats of Republican candidates in their state's Senate and gubernatorial races on Wednesday.

In an op-ed published in The Wall Street Journal, titled " Republicans Forgot How to Win Elections ," Cornyn said the GOP failed on four fronts in the midterms: broad voter appeal, candidate likeability, ability to deliver on promises and integrity.

"This week's beat-down wasn't only foreseeable, it was foreseen," the Republican, who lost his reelection primary bid to Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, added.

Cruz warned that Texans would be "hurt" after Democratic state Reps. James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa won the state's Senate and gubernatorial races, respectively.

"Texas is blue. That is a hard sentence to utter," the senator wrote on social media . "But Texas, today at least, is blue."

He continued, "As we sit here today, I am the only statewide elected Republican who remains in Texas. That's not something I ever thought I would say."

articles.title: Midterms might signal 'new era' for US-Israel relationship
articles.summary: Trump, who for months asked voters to pretend like he was on the ballot, heard loud and clear from them as Democrats swept Congress.
articles.body:
On Nov. 3, Election Day, Trump announced he had reached a deal to cut off aid to Israel by the end of the year.

By the following day — once the magnitude of Republican midterm losses became apparent — the question of how the U.S. relationship with Israel fit into Trump's "America First" promise and the price increases driven by the war with Iran was at the center of widespread GOP hand-wringing about where the party goes from here.

At the same time, the midterms ushered into Congress a slate of Democrats vocally critical of Israel, expanding their ranks in the Capitol.

Trump's first appearance since midterms at ballroom construction site

What was once an area of bipartisan consensus, American support for Israel has gone through a sea change in the aftermath of the Hamas attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, that killed about 1,200 people and took 251 people hostage and Israel's response, which has left tens of thousands of people in Gaza dead.

The midterms provided perhaps the clearest sign yet of how far public and political opinion on the U.S.-Israel relationship has shifted on both sides of the aisle.

"It's entering a new era and is still being defined," said Joel Rubin, a former deputy assistant Secretary of State for Legislative Affairs in the Obama administration. "Historically, the relationship has had strong bipartisan backing for decades. But both parties are now reviewing their way forward, as is Israel itself."

Trump, who for months asked voters to "pretend" he was on the ballot, heard loud and clear from them as Democrats swept Congress, ending a Republican trifecta. The scramble to understand what happened started almost immediately.

As the thrashing the GOP received became apparent, Trump said in an interview that "a part of it was Iran."

Vice President JD Vance , in a post on X , was blunt, writing: "The reason we lost is the war."

Vance also wrote that a trusted pollster had asked Trump 2024 voters planning to vote Democratic in 2026 what would convince them to return to the Republican fold. The four answers, according to Vance, were ending the war, focusing on cost-of-living issues, putting "America First" and changing "our relationship to Israel."

The war in Iran, which the U.S. and Israel launched in February, has upended global oil markets and contributed to a sharp increase in gas prices. Polls ahead of the midterms regularly found that economic and cost-of-living issues were the top voter concern.

But among a faction within Trump's Make America Great Again (MAGA) coalition, the skepticism toward Israel ran deeper.

For months, the MAGA brand of populists who adhere to the "America First" philosophy, such as former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, former Trump White House strategist Steve Bannon and conservative commentator Tucker Carlson, had been loudly critical of the ongoing military and financial assistance to Israel.

Bannon, for instance, said a resumption of major combat operations in Iran would infuriate the anti-interventionist MAGA base and result in internal political fallout.

Greene said the GOP had "turned its back on America First and the workers."

Trump, for his part, cast his Election Day announcement in a political light. He said in an interview on Nov. 3 that Israel is a thriving country and doesn't need the assistance, and described the aid as just a "bad talking point" that opens Republicans to "the slings from lunatics" like Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, the progressive Democrat who was elected in Michigan.

The White House did not respond to questions about a potential change in relationship between the two countries, instead referring the reporter to comments from Trump and Vance.

It was not just the MAGA influencers that appear to have soured on U.S. aid to Israel.

A recent public opinion survey by the Chicago Council on Public Affairs found that 56% of Americans favored decreasing or stopping military aid to Israel (broken down by 72% of Democrats, 65% of Independents, and 30% of Republicans).

A YouGov and AJP (Americans for Justice in Palestine) Action poll in April found that 56% of MAGA supporters support conditions on aid to Israel and that when it comes to foreign aid generally, 70% believe the U.S. should prioritize domestic needs.

While Israel is the largest cumulative recipient of U.S. foreign aid since 1946, Ukraine currently is the largest yearly beneficiary, having received $6.75 billion in 2025.

Podcaster Joe Rogan, who has a largely young male audience, is credited with helping Trump reach those voters in the lead-up to the 2024 presidential election.

In the 2024 presidential election, young voters supported the Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris by a 4-point margin, a much smaller margin than the 25-point support young voters gave Joe Biden in 2020. Young white men drove most of that shift, with many who voted for Biden in 2020 voting Republican in 2024, according to an analysis by the Center for Information and Research on Civic Learning and Engagement at Tufts University. That group represented one of the biggest swings back toward Democrats in 2026.

Rogan has criticized the Iran war, accusing the Trump administration of breaking its "no more wars" campaign promise and suggesting that U.S. involvement is driven by Israeli interests and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

William F.B. O'Reilly, a Republican strategist from New York, called this change in posture towards Israel "alarming" for both the U.S. and Israel.

"There is an unserious isolationist faction growing on the political right, led by Vice President Vance, that erroneously thinks America can stand alone in the world. It can't," he said. "Israel may be able to stand on her own economically, but its future is undeniably tied to ours. These are frightening times on both shores."

He said Vance's "less-than-subtle digs at Israel" can lead to greater attacks on that nation.

Democrats are struggling with their own rifts over Israel.

A New York Times/Siena poll found in May that three-quarters of Democratic voters opposed U.S. economic or military support for Israel.

That sentiment may be growing in Congress as well.

El-Sayed, an outspoken critic of U.S. military aid to Israel and other countries, who argued on the campaign trail that taxpayer dollars should be used to prioritize domestic needs like healthcare and education, was elected to the U.S. Senate from Michigan.

Israel emerged as a central issue in the Democratic primary between progressive El-Sayed and moderate Rep. Haley Stevens, and she pointed to his criticism of Israel in endorsing El-Sayed's GOP opponent days before the primary.

In New York, a trio of democratic socialist far-left candidates won their Democratic primaries this summer, ousting incumbents or besting candidates who were themselves progressive on many issues. The contests largely turned on support for Israel and all three nominees cruised to victory on Nov. 3.

Meanwhile, Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia, who was reelected, has adopted a balanced stance on U.S. military aid to Israel, supporting select defense systems while voting to block certain offensive weapons.

Those wins follow nearly half of House Democrats voting in July to cut off aid to Israel through an amendment to the State Department spending bill, signaling a lack of political support for a longtime ally. The measure did not pass due to lack of support from Republicans.

"Congressional Democrats, who overwhelmingly oppose the war with Iran and have deep concerns about the status of the Palestinian people, will enter the fray with real legislative powers," Rubin said. "There's a vibrant debate right now inside the Democratic Party over the future direction of the bilateral relationship, and both the pro-and anti-Israel wings won yesterday."

As for the MAGA base, Rubin said, while they are upset about military adventurism abroad, including the Iran war and the Venezuela intervention, it was a pale second in impact on their voting decision, when compared to affordability issues.

S wapna Venugopal Ramaswamy is a White House correspondent for USA TODAY. You can follow her on X @SwapnaVenugopal

articles.title: El partido más emotivo del Mundial de pádel: una leyenda argentina contra su hijo
articles.standfirst: Gaby Reca, seleccionador de la albiceleste, se medirá a su hijo Agustín, que juega con Alemania, en los cuartos de final
articles.summary: Gaby Reca, seleccionador de la albiceleste, se medirá a su hijo Agustín, que juega con Alemania, en los cuartos de final
articles.body: Gaby Reca, uno de los mejores jugadores de la historia del pádel profesional, tendrá el corazón dividido en los cuartos de final del Mundial celebrado en Doha. Como seleccionador y argentino, intentará que la albiceleste, gran favorita en la eliminatoria, gane sin problemas. Sin embargo, una parte de él también estará en el otro lado de la pista, pues Agustín, su hijo, defiende los colores de Alemania como jugador: un duelo familiar en el que solo uno podrá salir vencedor. Gaby es uno de los entrenadores más laureados del circuito. Entrena a varias figuras de Premier Padel y ejerce también como seleccionador de Argentina junto a Rodri Ovide. Además, durante su carrera cosechó numerosos títulos, alcanzando el liderato del ranking a comienzos de siglo. Agustín, nacido en el 2003, ocupa el número 170 del mundo y ha competido en varios de los torneos más importantes del calendario. En el Mundial, en cambio, pelearán el uno contra el otro. Que el pequeño de los Reca pueda jugar con Alemania se debe al origen de su familia: “Es por parte materna. Mi madre es alemana y como con Argentina, vamos a ser honestos, es difícil que juegue, se me abrió una puerta”, tal y como explica él mismo. Allí, ejerce como uno de los principales líderes del equipo: “Tengo el rol de subir el nivel de todo al jugar en torneos locales. Hablo con ellos, les doy consejos… Cumplo ese papel”. Y es que el papel de Alemania en este Mundial está siendo excepcional. Se trata de un país con muy poca tradición en este deporte que en los últimos años ha crecido a pasos agigantados, contando con citas del más alto nivel —como el P2 de Düsseldorf— y con varios jugadores llegando a rondas finales en Premier Padel y en el circuito FIP. Todo ello ha culminado con una clasificación a los cuartos de final por primera vez en su historia. Así pues, se verán las caras con la gran favorita (junto a España) a ganar el torneo en busca de un billete a las semifinales. Y, aunque Agustín tuvo que renunciar a su representación deportiva con Argentina, no es algo que moleste a su padre: “No es que se lo tomara bien o mal, sino que fue él quien tuvo la idea. Me dijo que probara con esto de Alemania. Le escuché y bueno… Le escucho poco, pero de vez en cuando le hago caso”. Una reunión familiar sobre una pista de pádel en la que tanto el hijo como el padre pelearán por seguir avanzando en el torneo. Una curiosa historia que regala este Mundial, el cual se acerca progresivamente a su épico desenlace.

articles.title: Republican AGs stand ready as 'last line of defense' against leftist policies after dismal midterms for party
articles.summary: Republican Attorneys General Association memo reveals GOP AG candidates ran 4.62 points ahead of Senate hopefuls across key midterm election states.
articles.body:
Republican attorney general candidates outperformed other midterm GOP hopefuls in several key races, according to a post-election analysis from the Republican Attorneys General Association, which urged colleagues to view their role as the "front line" against leftist policies following results that were likened to a "category-five political hurricane."

"America needs Republican Attorneys General now more than ever," RAGA Executive Director Adam Piper wrote in a late-night memo to colleagues shared with Fox News Digital. "With an emboldened Democrat Congress, Republican AGs are both America's front line and is the last line of defense when it comes to their left-wing wish list – such as court packing, the Green New Deal , Medicare for All, Second Amendment restrictions, and abolishing ICE."

Piper, who has worked in Virginia and on the staff of South Carolina Gov.-elect Alan Wilson, noted midterm election results showed Republican attorneys general candidates holding up slightly better on ballots despite a difficult Tuesday night for the party.

"Last night was the worst election night for the Republican Party in 50 years," Piper's memo began, acknowledging a difficult midterm "environment" that was ultimately made worse. "Last night, voters, regardless of party, preferred Democrat candidates by a mean of D +13.8 compared to D +7.9 in 2006 and D +8.4 in 2018.

"Today, we are dealing with the aftermath of a category-five political hurricane. It will take years to fully rebuild."

As Republicans are picking up the pieces and evaluating the map overcome with blue, even along wide swaths of Texas' southern border, the party is looking to the slight holds in Florida and any other silver linings.

Attorneys general might have something in the way of a pep talk for the party from Piper's memo.

GOP AG candidates ran an average of 4.62 percentage points ahead of GOP Senate candidates in comparable states and 2.12 points ahead of Republican gubernatorial candidates , according to the returns as of the late Wednesday night memo.

Republican AG candidates posted better margins than GOP Senate candidates in nine of 10 comparable states and outperformed Republican gubernatorial candidates in nine of 13 states, Piper wrote.

Still, Piper made clear that "there are no moral victories." Republicans did lose five AG seats to Democrats in these midterms , compared to a projected net loss of 51 in the House and a potential net loss of nine Senate seats.

Iowa, Ohio and Colorado were among the widest outperformers. The Republican attorney general candidates in those states ran 9.3, 7.3 and 10.3 points ahead of their party's gubernatorial candidates, respectively. In Colorado, the GOP attorney general candidate also outpaced the Republican Senate candidate by 7.7 points.

In Florida, now the largest red state with the handing over of Texas to the Democratic Party, Republican Attorney General James Uthmeier won by 1.8 percentage points, outperforming Gov.-elect Byron Donalds, who won by 1.3 points.

Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers won re-election by 12.6 points, compared with a 6.7-point win for Republican Senate candidate Pete Ricketts and an 8.4-point victory for Republican Gov. Jim Pillen .

RAGA spent more than $40 million on these midterms, nearly twice its spending in 2022, and was on track to raise more than $50 million, according to Piper.

"No amount of outperformance can make up for the historical Republican losses," his memo concluded. "RAGA will start to candidate recruit for 2027 and 2028 now and has set the expectation that we will continue to overperform, no matter the environment."

Republican midterm dissatisfaction will have a lasting impact on the party, but the executive director of the Republican Attorneys General Association is urging its colleagues to hold the "front line" against the Democrats' "category-five hurricane" of sweeping blue takeovers.

articles.title: Trump: Alaska’s incumbent GOP senator would ‘easily’ win if given ‘fake’ challenger’s votes
articles.summary: President Donald Trump on Thursday said Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan should be given votes cast for what he called "the Fake Dan Sullivan" also on the Alaska...
articles.body:
President Donald Trump on Thursday said Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan would "easily" win the Alaska Senate race if he was given the votes from the other candidate on the ballot who bears nearly the same name.

"The vote totals for the Fake Dan Sullivan, plus the other 'slug' that the Dems put on the Ballot, should be immediately given to the REAL Dan Sullivan, and the Election is over - He easily wins. There is no other fair solution!" Trump said in a post on Truth Social.

Despite bruising Republican Election Day losses across the country, it's the first time Trump has raised the idea of any voting irregularities.

Trump has no power to dictate election procedures, which the Constitution delegates to state governments . Still, he has spent the last several months pushing the federal government to exert control over election administration, including states' ability to manage voter rolls and count or administer mail-in ballots , which courts have batted down .

The other candidate Trump referenced is Daniel J. Sullivan, and his inclusion has for some time fueled concerns that it could confuse voters in the competitive race.

The Alaska Senate race has yet to be called, as the state continues to count remaining mail-in ballots. Democrat Mary Peltola holds a small lead with nearly 80% of the vote in, but if neither candidate receives a majority of the vote, a ranked-choice tabulation will take place on Nov. 18.

Last month, DOJ filed a lawsuit seeking to block Alaska election officials from certifying the results if the Republican incumbent Sullivan lost to Peltola. That lawsuit was dismissed earlier this week, though the Justice Department appealed.

The president, so far, has not asked the Justice Department to take further action.

articles.title: Midterms over, Democrats plunge into wide-open 2028 presidential race
articles.summary: By Tim Reid WASHINGTON, Nov 5 (Reuters) - With the US midterms over, Democrats are turning to what could become one of their most crowded and unpredictable p...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Nov 5 (Reuters) - With the US midterms over, Democrats are turning to what could become one of their most crowded and unpredictable presidential primaries in decades, a 2028 contest likely to expose the party's divide over how to win back the White House.

No Democrat has emerged as a clear favorite in a field that could attract dozens of contenders, while Republicans ‌have a smaller group of widely discussed candidates, led by Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, to succeed President Donald Trump, who is constitutionally barred from seeking a third term.

Potential Democratic ‌candidates, including sitting governors and senators, have spent months cultivating donors, visiting states with early nominating contests and raising their national profiles, positioning themselves for a race that strategists expect to begin in earnest now that the midterms are over.

The sweeping victories by Democrats on Tuesday, when voters ​delivered a sharp rebuke to Trump and his agenda, will intensify discussions within both parties about how to win over an electorate unhappy with the country's direction.

Despite their resounding victories on Tuesday, Democrats enter the 2028 campaign still divided over whether to tack to the center or move further left on issues ranging from healthcare and taxes to policing and foreign policy.

Republican candidates will face a different challenge – how to distance themselves from Trump after Tuesday's repudiation of his policies. They need to broaden their appeal beyond the president's base while avoiding a break with the populist Make America Great Again movement that has come to define the party.

Trump, who has dominated the political landscape for a decade, may be reluctant to yield center ‌stage, and his continued influence with MAGA followers could complicate the path of ⁠the party's next standard-bearer.

Doug Sosnik, a Democratic strategist, said both progressives and moderates will claim vindication in their ideological approaches, ensuring an intense internal battle over the party's future as the 2028 race begins in earnest.

One of the most high-profile progressive wins came in the Michigan Senate contest, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed easily defeated Republican Mike Rogers in a ⁠likely 2028 presidential swing state, becoming the first Muslim elected to the US Senate.

"All kinds of wings of the Democratic Party can find affirmation in the results last night," Sosnik said on Wednesday. "I don't think that anyone can, nor should they, try to contain the differences we have as a party."

Several potential candidates have either acknowledged considering a White House run or declined to rule one out. Most spent the final weeks of the midterm campaign stumping for fellow Democrats in early nominating states such as Nevada, ​New ​Hampshire and South Carolina.

They include former Vice President Kamala Harris, who lost to Trump in 2024, Governors Gavin Newsom of California and ​Andy Beshear of Kentucky, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, and US Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of ‌New York, a leading progressive voice.

Reuters contacted representatives for nine of the party's most prominent potential contenders. None confirmed a 2028 run.

Nine days after the November 3 elections, several prospective Democratic candidates, including Buttigieg and another progressive, US Representative Ro Khanna of California, are scheduled to attend a gathering in Denver hosted by Majority Democrats.

The group, backed largely by moderate Democrats and billionaire donor Steve Mandel, advocates for younger party leaders and a party platform that is more centrist.

US Representative Jake Auchincloss of Massachusetts, the group's chair, said the event is meant to spark a debate about the party's future before the 2028 race takes shape, and lay out a positive agenda for what the party is for, rather than just being anti-Trump.

Scott Ferson, a Democratic strategist, said the party's presidential primary could attract a huge number of candidates. "There are at least 30 Democrats who are saying to people close to them, 'Do you think I should run?'" ‌Ferson said.

By contrast, Republican 2028 hopefuls have been more guarded, mostly staying in Trump's shadow and deferential to him.

That ​could now change after Tuesday night's rout in which voters expressed deep dissatisfaction with Trump's handling of the economy and foreign policy and ​demanded more action against government corruption.

Vance is in a particularly difficult position, said Matt Dole, a Republican strategist. ​Vance has less freedom than other potential 2028 Republican contenders to put daylight between himself and Trump because he is vice president, a role that traditionally involves defending the president and ‌his policies.

"Vance just doesn't have the wiggle room that somebody else in the cabinet ​has, who can resign," Dole said.

Still, Vance acknowledged on Wednesday ​that the war in Iran, which Trump launched in February and which is deeply unpopular among Americans, had cost Republicans the election. That, however, did not represent a clear break with Trump, who made a similar acknowledgement on Tuesday night.

Whoever emerges within the Republican Party as its new standard-bearer will face the task of keeping Trump's MAGA base onside while rebuilding the broader coalition that powered his 2024 victory. Exit polls ​on Tuesday showed that key constituencies of that coalition, including younger voters, Hispanics and ‌some Black men, had deserted Republicans.

Vance has said there is "a chance" he will not run, citing family considerations, while Rubio has said he has "no plans at this time" to seek the presidency.

Florida Governor ​Ron DeSantis, who unsuccessfully sought the Republican presidential nomination against Trump in 2024, has declined to rule out another White House bid.

Other Republicans viewed as potential candidates include Arkansas Governor Sarah Huckabee ​Sanders and US Senator Ted Cruz of Texas.

articles.title: Alaska, Mississippi Senate races separated by razor-thin vote margins
articles.summary: "Decoy Dan" Sullivan garnered 3,600 votes in the Alaska Senate race, far dwarfing the 642-vote margin between Dan Sullivan and Mary Peltola.
articles.body: Races between the candidates for U.S. Senate in Alaska and Mississippi are separated by razor-thin margins days after polls closed in the crucial midterm elections. In Mississippi, where 95.6% of the votes have been counted, according to the Associated Press, Democratic candidate Scott Colom leads incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, R-Miss., 464,926 votes to 463,788, as of Thursday morning. In Alaska, former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola, leads incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, by less than 700 votes. DOJ SET TO APPEAL RULING IN ALASKA SENATE RACE DISPUTE OVER ‘DECOY DAN’ While Alaska still has a quarter of its votes to count, according to the AP, if the gap between Peltola and Sullivan remains this slim, the introduction of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan will loom large in post-election analyses. In July, the U.S. Justice Department opened an investigation into Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired schoolteacher who entered the Senate race in May. TRUMP PROSECUTIONS UNDER BIDEN SET PRECEDENT FOR DOJ’S ALASKA ‘DECOY DAN’ PROBE, EX-FEC CHAIR SAYS An October report from The New York Times said Daniel J. Sullivan had met with Democratic operatives and members of Peltola's campaign staff to encourage him to run. Peltola has denied any involvement in the scheme. One voter interviewed after he cast his ballot Tuesday revealed that he believed he accidentally voted for the wrong Dan Sullivan. MARY PELTOLA'S CAMPAIGN, DEMS BACKED COVERT SCHEME TO FIELD SPOILER CANDIDATES IN ALASKA SENATE RACE: REPORT "I don't remember seeing the other Dan Sullivan, I totally forgot to look for two Dan Sullivans," the bewildered voter revealed. "I definitely intended to vote for the real Dan Sullivan." As of Thursday morning, Daniel J. Sullivan, aka "Decoy Dan," had garnered 3,600 votes from Alaskans, a number that's more than five times larger than the 637-vote margin separating Sen. Sullivan and Peltola. PELTOLA CAMPAIGN'S ALLEGED DAN SULLIVAN SPOILER PLOT TAKES NEW TURN AS DOJ FACES MAJOR LEGAL HURDLE Under Alaska's ranked choice voting system, if no candidate achieves a 50% share of the vote, the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated and voters who chose that candidate first will have their votes redirected to their second choice. President Donald Trump weighed in on the saga, demanding Daniel J. Sullivan's votes be given to Sen. Sullivan. "The vote totals for the Fake Dan Sullivan, plus the other 'slug' that the Dems put on the Ballot, should be immediately given to the REAL Dan Sullivan, and the Election is over - He easily wins," Trump wrote in a Thursday morning post on Truth Social. "There is no other fair solution! President DJT" he concluded. GOVERNOR PROBING 'DECOY DAN' SULLIVAN ELECTION SCANDAL WARNS SYSTEM FLAW HIDING IN PLAIN SIGHT In Mississippi, officials are still waiting to receive a batch of 3,600 mail-in ballots, according to a statement from Secretary of State Michael Watson. The state allows mail-in ballots to be counted if they're received within five business days of the election, provided they were postmarked with a date of the election day or earlier. NBC News' Decision Desk pegs the remaining ballots to be counted at 45,000. TIM SCOTT DECLARES ALLEGED 'DECOY DAN' PLOT A 'CRIMINAL OFFENSE' AS DOJ INVESTIGATION ROCKS ALASKA Mississippi has no formal process for recounts, making a legal fight over the results increasingly likely. "We will protect the process of this election, we'll protect the integrity of this election," Colom told reporters Wednesday, adding that he had "an army of lawyers" preparing for a court battle, Mississippi Public Broadcasting reported. ALASKA'S GOVERNOR ORDERS INVESTIGATION AFTER NYT REPORT ON ALLEGED DEM-LINKED SENATE ELECTION SCHEME Hyde-Smith's team, meanwhile, remains assured that the sitting senator will prevail. "Our campaign is closely monitoring the remaining count," campaign manager Scott Monssen told MPB in a statement. "We remain confident that when every legally cast vote is fully and accurately counted, Mississippians will have reelected Cindy Hyde-Smith," he concluded. articles.title: A midterm election defeat too overwhelming for Trump to challenge?
articles.summary: Experts say months of prep, mobilization by election watchers – and a massive Democratic victory – helped stave off efforts to influence the midterms.
articles.body:
WASHINGTON – Months of warnings that the Trump administration would send armed agents to the polls, seize voting machines or try to undermine Democratic victories largely came to nothing on Election Day .

All the preparation and turnout by local elections officials, lawyers and voting rights organizations helped ensure that any Trump administration attempts to overstep were quickly halted, according to David Becker, a former DOJ official and election integrity expert.

"For all of the handwringing and speculation about how the federal government might interfere, how foreign adversaries might attempt to interfere … we're seeing elections go very normally, with only minor problems," Becker, founder and executive director of the Center for Election Innovation & Research, told reporters on Election Day.

Later, Becker singled out election officials nationwide for doing their jobs despite "a turbulent, and at times hostile, political environment."

"In the past year, election officials have faced legal threats from the administration, the withdrawal of federal resources that previously supported their work, and intense public scrutiny," Becker said. "They withstood all those challenges to get the job done for their voters today."

Above all, Becker and other experts said, the sheer size of the Democratic victory left the Trump administration and its allies with too few legal options and too little to contest.

Trump himself shut down talk of rejecting the results Tuesday night, telling The New York Times that he was "absolutely willing to accept those results." So far, Trump hasn't claimed fraud in the midterm elections, instead writing on Truth Social that he "wasn't on the Ballot" and would otherwise have won "IN A LANDSLIDE!"

Democrats celebrate blue tsunami. See the historic moment

Aarti Kohli, executive director of the Asian Law Caucus, said her organization's monitors reported long lines and language access issues, but none of the election interference issues they feared.

"So far our monitors are reporting what we hoped to see: voters voting, poll workers helping them and problems getting fixed," she said.

Before the election, Democratic state attorneys general, local governments and voting rights advocates very publicly went to court early and often.

And federal judges repeatedly reined in Justice Department efforts to intervene in election processes that under the Constitution are supposed to be run by state and local officials. For example, judges, and ultimately the Supreme Court , rejected DOJ's bid to force California to set aside mail-in ballots from about 20,000 voters it alleged were "likely" noncitizens.

The DOJ has also lost more than two dozen court cases in which it sought full statewide voter files, according to Democracy Docket.

State governments and voting rights advocates spent months preparing for the worst, with Democratic lawyers war-gaming various scenarios in which the Trump administration might seek to intervene and overstep its authority.

Cities, counties and civil rights groups sued to keep armed ICE agents away from polling places, and tens of thousands of volunteers showed up to monitor the polls on Election Day. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin confirmed late on Election Day that his agency had sent no Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents to polling locations.

For months, DOJ said it would send election monitors to polling places, and it did, deploying about 1,000, in what DOJ officials said was its largest-ever effort.

In Michigan, home to one of the most hotly contested Senate races, DOJ monitors asked poll workers in Dearborn and Flint about their training and requested training materials. After the Michigan Department of State said that was "not permitted under the law," DOJ agreed and said it would inform the monitors .

In New Mexico, the secretary of state's office said monitors in Bernalillo County were "asking some unusual questions and doing things that are not allowed by law such as questioning voters." DOJ later said it believed "the issue is resolved."

"Right now, we are not seeing the kind of large-scale systemic interference that we were prepared for," Leah Greenberg, co-founder of the progressive group Indivisible, told USA TODAY on Election Day.

Trump had long hinted he might order the seizure of voting machines or ballots, following his longstanding – and unfounded – assertions that the 2020 election he lost to Joe Biden was rigged. FBI agents in January executed a warrant and seized 2020 ballots and other records in Fulton County, Georgia, in a search for evidence of that. That same month, Trump also told The New York Times he regretted not ordering the National Guard to seize voting machines after that loss.

No federal seizures of voting machines or ballots were reported on Election Day.

Yet there are still opportunities for the federal government to challenge the results.

A federal judge in Anchorage dismissed DOJ's lawsuit seeking to preemptively block certification of Alaska's Senate race featuring two candidates named Dan Sullivan – one is the Republican incumbent and one is a retired schoolteacher – and Democrat Mary Peltola. The DOJ is appealing that decision and has escalated a criminal investigation into whether Democrats recruited the retired teacher to confuse voters. Peltola's campaign has denied involvement.

Results in Alaska's Senate race are still pending. And California will count ballots for at least several days, according to its vote-by-mail deadlines.
